For this reason, depth in a network holds a lot of its power. It allows repeated iteration and refinement of features. And it allows it to happen with increasing amounts of abstraction and complexity. Where a first block might resolve surface relationships based on just word meanings, the second block could build an understanding of a word based on how another word in the sentence was contextualized by a different word. And so on, the relationships continue to get complex the deeper you go! Each block builds more abstract structure on top of the understanding the previous ones already formed, building up richer and richer understanding of all of the nuances a token holds as it goes.

Back to our architecture, let’s flesh out the encoder, which we now understand to really look like:

And that, really, is the encoder’s output and the value it brings. The encoder’s job isn’t to produce any language or make any predictions. It’s just to create one vector per token that carries deep, contextualized understanding of that token and its meaning, in the context of the entire sequence.

3.3 A Real Encoder: BERT

So we’ve seen all of the pieces come together. But let’s confirm it in a real, trained encoder.

To do this, we’ll look at what comes out of the encoder-only model BERT. BERT (“Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers”) was introduced by Google in late 2018, and it’s one of the most influential models in NLP history. For a few years it was the backbone of an enormous amount of language understanding work, including Google Search itself. For our purposes, we’re choosing it because it’s small and its architecture was simple. It is essentially exactly the encoder stack we just worked through.

The specific model we’re loading, bert-base-uncased, is very small by today’s standards, but at the time was quite large. It contains:

  • ~110 million parameters
  • 12 stacked encoder blocks
  • 12 attention heads per block
  • \(d_{model} = 768\)
  • vocabulary of ~30,000 subword tokens
  • maximum sequence length of 512

(The “uncased” just means it lowercases text before tokenizing.)

BERT was pre-trained on a huge pile of unlabeled text (English Wikipedia plus a large corpus of books, roughly 3 billion words). Its training objective was masked language modeling, which essentially means trying to “fill in the blank”. Random words in each sentence were replaced with [MASK], and the model learned to predict what word was supposed to be there. Because it always got to see the full surrounding context - the whole sequence both before and after the masked word - it is very good at building those rich, context-aware representations. (We’ll talk more about model flavors (encoder only, decoder only, encoder-decoders) after we’ve gone through the decoder section below, but for now just note that BERT was never trained to generate new text at all - it only ever learned to understand so that it could fill in. It was trained, precisely, just to be a good encoder.)

Just to note, a few things do differ from the exact architecture we laid out. All of these are small tweaks, which we already discussed as we went along that these common alternatives exist.

  1. BERT uses learned positional encodings (a trainable table), rather than the sinusoidal version that we discussed in depth from the original paper.
  2. It uses post-norm (LayerNorm after the residual add - like the original paper), where in this tutorial we chose to present the pre-norm that is more common in modern times.
  3. Its feed-forward networks use GELU rather than ReLU (the smoothed version we mentioned in Appendix 3).
  4. It tokenizes with WordPiece rather than BPE. WordPiece is a similar subword tokenizer, that proceeds in a similar way as BPE, but optimizes for some slightly different things as it does its merges.

None of these significantly change the major points of what we just discussed - they’re all examples of small, practical changes and choices that exist in the landscape of building an encoder. All of the building blocks are exactly the same.

We’ll use BERT to look at the following two sentences:

\[ \textit{The river bank was flooded after the storm.} \]

and

\[ \textit{I deposited my paycheck at the bank downtown.} \]

An encoder that’s doing its job should have very different interpretations of the word “bank” in those two sentences - as they have entirely different meanings that can only be determined by looking at how they’re used in the sentence as a whole. Let’s look at what BERT gives us to confirm if that’s true.

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
model.eval()   # (this downloads the model the first time - it may take a minute)

def bank_vectors(sentence):
    enc    = tokenizer(sentence, return_tensors="pt")
    tokens = tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(enc["input_ids"][0])
    pos    = tokens.index("bank")               # 'bank' is a single token in BERT's vocab
    with torch.no_grad():
        before = model.embeddings.word_embeddings(enc["input_ids"])[0][pos]  # context-FREE
        after  = model(**enc).last_hidden_state[0][pos]                      # context-AWARE
    return before, after

river_in, river_out = bank_vectors("the river bank was flooded after the storm")
money_in, money_out = bank_vectors("i deposited my paycheck at the bank downtown")

print("BEFORE the encoder (raw embedding lookup):")
print("  cosine of the two 'bank' vectors:", round(F.cosine_similarity(river_in, money_in, dim=0).item(), 4))
print("AFTER the encoder (contextual representation):")
print("  cosine of the two 'bank' vectors:", round(F.cosine_similarity(river_out, money_out, dim=0).item(), 4))

BEFORE the encoder (raw embedding lookup):
  cosine of the two 'bank' vectors: 1.0
AFTER the encoder (contextual representation):
  cosine of the two 'bank' vectors: 0.4063

Before the encoder, the two “bank” vectors are identical - same token, same row of the embedding table. After the encoder, they’ve been pulled apart, because one absorbed “river…flooded” and the other “deposited…paycheck.” Same word in, two different meanings out. That is the whole job of the encoder in one measurement: it turns context-free lookups into context-aware representations.

We can go one step further and check the split is meaningful - the river-“bank” should sit closer to water words, the money-“bank” closer to finance words:

def contextual(sentence, word):
    enc = tokenizer(sentence, return_tensors="pt")
    tks = tokenizer.convert_ids_to_tokens(enc["input_ids"][0])
    with torch.no_grad():
        return model(**enc).last_hidden_state[0][tks.index(word)]

water = contextual("the boat drifted down the river", "river")
cash  = contextual("i keep my cash in the account", "cash")

print("river-'bank' vs 'river':", round(F.cosine_similarity(river_out, water, dim=0).item(), 3))
print("river-'bank' vs 'cash' :", round(F.cosine_similarity(river_out, cash,  dim=0).item(), 3))
print("money-'bank' vs 'river':", round(F.cosine_similarity(money_out, water, dim=0).item(), 3))
print("money-'bank' vs 'cash' :", round(F.cosine_similarity(money_out, cash,  dim=0).item(), 3))
river-'bank' vs 'river': 0.429
river-'bank' vs 'cash' : 0.342
money-'bank' vs 'river': 0.314
money-'bank' vs 'cash' : 0.428

4. The Decoder

So, great! The encoder has done its job. It understands the input, and turns our sequence of words into a set of rich, contextualized representations. But that rich embedding of the input sequence isn’t really a usable output as-is. If we wanted to say, output the next word we think will come, or translate that sequence into a different language, nothing the encoder produced is actually a word, a next token, or an answer. It’s “just” a pile of meaning-laden vectors. If we want to do any of the tasks that require us to actually produce language, we need another half of the architecture: the decoder.

The good news is that most of the building blocks here are largely reused, so we don’t need to define and understand a bunch more components. But, there are two new ideas on the decoder side that the encoder didn’t need, and those are causal masking and cross-attention. So despite the decoder being the “second half” of the model, the new conceptual work we’ll need to do is small, and these new concepts build strongly on the existing foundation we already have.

4.1 Why Two Halves?

Before we get to those new building blocks, it’s worth building the context as to why a full generation model is split cleanly into these encoder and decoder parts at all. And it’ll be useful to think of them as distinct parts, and what those distinct parts do differently, as actually many modern models are just one or the other, not two parts together.

The insight is that there are really two distinct things that have to happen to successfully model language:

  1. Understanding. To know how a language is built, what the words mean, how they relate, you have to be able to fully understand how sentences are constructed, why words go together and what order they do, what words can mean in different contexts, etc. This is the encoder’s job. Given a sequence, it looks at how the words relate in both directions - every token must attend to every other token, because comprehending a sentence requires seeing the whole thing. In the example at the end of the encoder section, “bank” is disambiguated by words on either side. Before you can do anything with language, you start by just knowing what it means. So its output is just rich representations.
  2. Generating. If you wanted to produce a new sequence, you have to do it one word (token) at a time, conditioned only on what came before. This is the decoder’s job. It needs to be able to look in one direction only - only at the words that come before - because when language is being produced, the words ahead don’t exist yet. So its output is actual tokens.

While a lot of the same concepts will be re-used, these two jobs are different enough that they can be separated entirely, and it mostly comes down to that “what do you get to look at” question. If to understand we must attend forward and backward, but to generate we can only attend backwards, we naturally have two fundamentally different ways that processing words can behave. But as it turns out, each half is useful on its own, and that’s why you’re likely to encounter three main flavors of transformer out in the world:

  • Encoder-only models (like BERT): Sometimes, the task only requires that you understand a sequence of words. For tasks like classification, sentiment analysis, searching, the point is just to get a good representation of the words, then use it. So you can run an encoder, take its representations, and attach a small task-specific head. If you assume you already “have” the words you’re working with, then there’s no generation, and no need for a decoder, at all.
  • Decoder-only (like GPT): Other times, you only need to do the generation, with each token conditioned on the past. As it turns out, most modern models are this, as this can also cover an enormous range, even including tasks that sound like understanding, so long as they’re reframed as generation tasks - (“[REVIEW]. The sentiment of this review is ___“). The job of a decoder-only model is really just to make more tokens, so you don’t need to understand something first, then generate, the understanding just needs to happen about the text you’re generating more of.
  • Encoder-decoder (the original Transformer, like T5): The full transformer architecture, both pieces, is really needed in tasks where you need to understand one thing completely, then generate a different thing from it. The classic example is translation - you need to read and understand the entire French sentence, then produce the English version one token at a time. This is the architecture we’re building in this tutorial, and translation is exactly the example we’ll use.

A decoder-only model like GPT might seem like it’s “doing both” jobs - it surely must see, process, and understand all text before deciding what to generate. In a sense, it is, but not by having two halves. It’s a single stack of masked self-attention blocks, trained from scratch without the separate encoder and cross-attention we’ll come to see. Most frontier models today are exactly this decoder-only.

And encoder-only models like BERT, which are trained in a “fill in the blank” type task (masked language modeling) also end in a token prediction, but are not generator models. The key difference, again, being that the context in all encoders is bidirectional, so the task is still about learning good representations.

At the end of the tutorial, we’ll talk more about exactly how these different model types are trained, so you can see exactly how these differences show up when building a real, modern model. For now, just keep in mind that the two halves do wind up being useful on their own, even though we’ll continue to think about the full encoder and decoder as doing separate things but connected into one architecture.

So in this tutorial, we’ll build the original, full encoder-decoder from Attention Is All You Need. All three of the above architecture types come out of it, so once you understand it fully, understanding exactly how the parts come to stand on their own becomes much simpler.

4.2 Causal Masking

The first new component we need to understand the full decoder architecture is causal masking, which will literally prevent the decoder portion of the model from giving any attention to certain parts of the sequence. This is an important feature that protects the decoder’s text generation from “cheating”, by making sure it only has access to and understanding of its previous tokens.

4.2.1 Autoregression

Before we get into exactly the math, let’s build some intuition about why we need this new component. The core idea is that a decoder must produce its output autoregressively - one token at a time, with every new token being a function of all those before it. The model’s own previous outputs become the input for producing the next token, over and over again.

For instance, say the decoder’s job is to produce a French-to-English translation. Then, production of the English sentence “I love cats”, will proceed one word at a time:

step 1:  [INPUT] <bos>                 -> [OUTPUT] "I"
step 2:  [INPUT] <bos> I               -> [OUTPUT] "love"
step 3:  [INPUT] <bos> I love          -> [OUTPUT] "cats"
step 4:  [INPUT] <bos> I love cats     -> [OUTPUT] <eos>   (stop)

Where <bos> and <eos> are special tokens that indicate the start/end of a generation sequence. The output is always a single next word, but the input grows with every word produced - the entire sequence so far goes back into the model to determine which next word to produce. It keeps generating, with every new word conditioned on everything generated so far (plus the encoder’s understanding, through cross-attention, which we’ll get to), until it produces the “end of sequence” token <eos> and stops.

The key difference between how the decoder and encoder get to process words is that the decoder, since its job is to generate one at a time, cannot attend to later positions since at generation time they simply don’t exist yet. And if we only ever ran the model in generation mode, producing one token at a time, this would always be the case and we wouldn’t need to worry about it. At step t, the input literally is only the tokens we’ve produced so far, so there’s nothing to “look ahead” at anyway.

The problem shows up at training time. Training one token at a time (constantly checking if every single individual token produced is the one we wanted) would be wastefully slow. Instead, we feed the decoder the entire known target sequence at once and check its prediction of the next token at every position in a single pass. The issue is that this means, when we go to see at position t, what token we predict at t+1, well the answer is already sitting right there at position t+1. If we didn’t do anything to cover up the later tokens, the model would just learn to go look at it.

Causal masking is what prevents this. It blocks each position from attending to anything after it, so even though the full sequence is present, every position only ever sees what’s behind it - exactly the information it would have during real generation. We get to process the whole sequence at once, without worrying about muddying up the whole point and premise of the decoder.

4.2.2 What the Mask Looks Like

It turns out that enforcing this is remarkably clean and easy to do - no complicated extra math. It winds up just being a triangular mask applied to the calculated attention that says “actually, don’t pay any attention to that”.

Recall that, coming out of the attention calculation, we have attention weights that come from a softmax over each query’s row of scores. For a sequence of length T, the score matrix: \[ S = QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k} \] is a \(T × T\) matrix, where row i says how the ith entry in the sequence should attend to each other position j. If we run this in the decoder, it’ll be completely filled in, including with how much attention a token at position 3 should attend to the token at position 5, even though that one is “in its future.”

Then, to prevent that, we can simply build a mask that says, for a token at position i, just ignore all of the attention scores to tokens for positions j > i. This is another matrix, the causal mask, which is also of size \(T × T\), but where entry (i, j) is 1 where i is allowed to see key j (that is, j ≤ i), and 0 otherwise. It ends up just being a lower-triangular block of ones:

          key1  key2  key3
query1:    1     0     0
query2:    1     1     0
query3:    1     1     1

Then, before we softmax the attention scores, we apply this mask to the attention score matrix, taking every disallowed entry of the score matrix and setting it to \(−\infty\):

scores = scores.masked_fill(mask == 0, -∞)

Why \(−\infty\), and why before softmax? Recall that softmax is:

\[\text{softmax}(s)_j = \frac{e^{s_j}}{\sum_k e^{s_k}}\]

To force a future position’s weight when the attention is actually applied to be exactly zero, \(e^{s_j}\) must be 0. This is only met when \(s_j = −\infty\). That part is easy to see. So why make sure we apply before softmax? The answer is to make sure the normalization is still right and the probability distribution still sums to 1. If we instead do softmax to get attention weights, then try to apply our mask and zero out the future weights, the weights will no longer sum to 1. But as we discussed in the attention section, this is important, so we’d have to re-normalize to make sure that they do. But that’s an extra step, and extra compute. Instead, setting this \(−\infty\) before the softmax means that the re-normalization happens as a part of that calculation, with the zeros getting no contribution already in the calculation of the probability distribution, to save us some work.

4.2.3 New Multi-Head Attention Code

Since this is so remarkably simple, it’s actually typically implemented right into the multi-head attention code, not as something independent. So while we already have MultiHeadAttention code above, we need to rewrite it with a small edit to reflect that it can also be, optionally, masked. That way this same code piece is reusable every time we need MHA.

And a quick note you’ll see as we’re about to implement this: in actual code we have to use a large negative number like -1e9 rather than literal -inf. This is because a literal -inf can produce a NaN in some cases, which will cause big problems, and e^{-1e9} is already zero to floating point precision anyway.

class MultiHeadAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, embed_size, heads):
        super(MultiHeadAttention, self).__init__()
        self.embed_size = embed_size
        self.heads = heads
        self.head_dim = embed_size // heads

        assert (self.head_dim * heads == embed_size), "Embedding size must be divisible by heads"

        self.values = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size, bias=False)
        self.keys = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size, bias=False)
        self.queries = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size, bias=False)
        self.fc_out = nn.Linear(embed_size, embed_size)

    def forward(self, values, keys, query, mask=None):              # <- NEW! We must have a mask option, default None
        N = query.shape[0]
        value_len, key_len, query_len = values.shape[1], keys.shape[1], query.shape[1]

        values  = self.values(values)
        keys    = self.keys(keys)
        queries = self.queries(query)

        values  = values.reshape(N, value_len, self.heads, self.head_dim)
        keys    = keys.reshape(N, key_len, self.heads, self.head_dim)
        queries = queries.reshape(N, query_len, self.heads, self.head_dim)

        values  = values.transpose(1, 2)
        keys    = keys.transpose(1, 2)
        queries = queries.transpose(1, 2)

        attention_scores = queries @ keys.transpose(-2, -1)
        attention_scores = attention_scores / (self.head_dim ** 0.5)

        if mask is not None:                                         # <- NEW! If we need the mask, apply it here
            attention_scores = attention_scores.masked_fill(mask == 0, -1e9)

        attention = torch.softmax(attention_scores, dim=-1)
        self.attention_weights = attention.detach()                  # <- (NEW - not mask related - save a copy to look at later)

        out = attention @ values

        out = out.transpose(1, 2).reshape(N, query_len, self.heads * self.head_dim)
        return self.fc_out(out)

One thing you might notice, is that we build MultiHeadAttention to take a mask instead of building one. This is really just for simplicity’s sake in the code. We want to be able to re-use this MultiHeadAttention definition in the encoder’s self-attention (with no mask), the decoder’s masked self-attention (with the causal mask we just discussed), and in the decoder’s cross-attention (which we’re about to see, is just another small edit to how the attention we already know is done). In each of these cases, the masking behavior is different. Passing the mask, whatever it needs to look like, is the simplest way of being able to use this definition in all 3 cases.

For causal masking, making the mask itself is done with a single line:

torch.tril(torch.ones(seq_len, seq_len))

Which is constructed once and passed down into each decoder block. We’ll come back to this, and see exactly where it’s defined and passed in, when we assemble a full decoder later in this section.

4.3 Cross Attention

So then, as we just alluded to, cross-attention will also just be a straightforward change to how we use the multi-head attention concepts that we already defined and already know. But let’s of course stop first to talk about what it’s meant to do.

For a task like French-English translation, and indeed any task that really requires the encoder-decoder architecture, there is a core insight: the whole point is that there’s something other that we had to understand in order to be able to generate this thing.

If we just started running the decoder part of a French-English translation model, as we saw above, it just starts with <bos>, and starts writing English text. How would it know to make “I love cats” over “I love dogs”? To start the sentence with “I” at all?

The answer, of course, is that we must connect it to the encoder and its understanding of “J’aime les chats”, and the way that is done is through cross-attention, which allows the tokens being produced in English to attend to the tokens that went through the encoder pipeline, and their rich, interconnected contextualization to each other. The decoder must, in order to produce “I”, be able to see how the encoder represents “J’”, which up until now has just gone through the encoder and sat there.

4.3.1 Back to Q, K, V

So what actually changes? Recall that in self-attention, the query, key, and value all come from the same sequence - every token asks a question about itself (Q), advertises what it offers (K), and carries its own content (V). Cross-attention uses those same interpretations of Q, K, and V, but now pulls its inputs from two different places:

  • The query comes from the decoder - the English sequence being generated. Each English position forms a query meaning, roughly, “given what I’m trying to produce next, what do I need from the French?”
  • The key and value both come from the encoder’s output - the contextualized French representations. Each French position offers a key (for matching against the decoder’s query) and a value (the content that gets pulled in if it matches).

Everything else is identical to the attention we already know. The scores are still computed as \(Q \cdot K^{\top}\), then scaled and softmaxed into a set of weights that sum to 1. The output is still a weighted sum of the values. The only difference is that the questions are being asked by one sequence (English) and answered by another (French). When the decoder is about to produce “cats,” its query lands most of its attention weight on the encoder’s representation of “chats,” and pulls that content into its own stream.

Now, there are two other major things to keep in mind that are a little different from how we’ve talked about attention so far, which we’ll see come to fruition in a real example later.

  1. The attention matrix will no longer be square. When we did self-attention, the attention scores were always square because seq_len was always the same - we were always working with the same sequence. But here, the English sequence is growing while the French sequence is a fixed size. So the attention matrix will come out to seq_len_o (output, English) × seq_len_i (input, French) .This isn’t a problem - nothing ever required attention to be square - self-attention was just a special case where the two sides happened to be the same sequence. The only consequence is that we’ll have two different sequence lengths that need to be tracked to make sure all of our sizes are right.
  2. We will not mask this at all. Causal masking is used at training time to be sure the decoder can’t look ahead. But here, the growing sequence is attending to something that will always be fully known - the French sequence is complete both at training time and at generation time. So even though this is another case of MHA in the decoder, it won’t need to be masked like the self-attention that comes just before it.

There’s one interesting thing to point out here, which might help hammer in the interpretations of Q, K, and V as distinct matrices which probe distinct things, that becomes a bit more clear when you see it in cross-attention.

We already alluded to it in the original MHA section, but notice that keys and values are a necessarily bonded pair. Whereas the query is free - it’s not required to match any other shape.

Look at the shapes. In the attention calculation, we begin with: \[ Q \ \ \in \ \ n_{\text{seq, 1}} \times d_{\text{model}} \] \[ K \ \ \in \ \ n_{\text{seq, 2}} \times d_{\text{model}} \] \[ V \ \ \in \ \ n_{\text{seq, 3}} \times d_{\text{model}} \]

Then, when we do \(Q K^{\top}\), the \(d_{\text{model}}\) becomes the interior dimension, so they are compatible regardless of what \(n_{\text{seq, 1}}\) and \(n_{\text{seq, 2}}\) are. The result is \(n_{\text{seq, 1}} \times n_{\text{seq, 2}}\).

But later, this result is multiplied by V: \[ O = A \times V \]

Then, this is a \(n_{\text{seq, 1}} \times n_{\text{seq, 2}}\) times an \(n_{\text{seq, 3}} \times d_{\text{model}}\) calculation. If \(n_{\text{seq, 3}} \neq n_{\text{seq, 2}}\), the math fundamentally fails, right there. So it’s mathematically forced that the keys and values must describe the same set of items, while the queries can come from somewhere else entirely. This is exactly what cross-attention exploits.

But it goes back to our intuitive interpretation of attention as a soft dictionary lookup as well. If our keys tell us “how you’d find an item”, and your values tell you “what you get from an item”, then they naturally are a bonded pair. Like a dictionary definition, and the word it belongs to (though attention allows us to quantify how much every potential word relates to every potential definition).

Still, the interpretation is that the key \(j\) and value \(j\) are two views of the same source token - as its searchable handle and its retrievable content. Though we produce them with different learned projections (\(W_K\) and \(W_V\)), they are bound to the same item. The query, by contrast, is flexible to ask about something else, which is why it’s so useful to do so in cross attention. We can ask about a different sequence, with a different length, or in a different language, and still get the right information that we need from the other two.

4.3.2 Cross-Attention in Code

As we already mentioned, our MultiHeadAttention class is actually already set up to support this change to cross attention without changing it at all - just by giving it different inputs.

Recall that when we did multi-head attention in the encoder, we passed the same value in 3 times to construct Q, K, and V. And in masked self-attention, we do the exact same thing with a mask.

# inside the decoder block's forward (x = decoder's own sequence, enc_out = encoder output):

# 1. how we did self-attention in the encoder: Q, K, V all = x, no causal mask
self_attn = self.attention(x, x, x)
# ...residual + norm...

# 2. masked self-attention in the decoder: Q, K, V all = x, with the causal mask
self_attn = self.attention(x, x, x, mask=trg_mask)
# ...residual + norm...

Well, in cross attention, we simply define the different sources that we need for Q, K, and V:

# 3. cross-attention: V and K come from the encoder, Q comes from the decoder
cross_attn = self.cross_attention(enc_out, enc_out, query)
#                                 └- V -┘  └- K -┘ └- Q -┘

In this case, \(V\) and \(K\), which remember must always be from the same source, come from the output of the encoder. We call this with no mask (for now, we’ll discuss a nuance in a bit), because remember - there’s no “cheating” about the known encoder information.

4.4 Building the Decoder

Now, we can assemble the decoder. The fortunate thing is that, the same way that the few extra pieces we went over were really just tweaks to things we already understood well, the decoder block is really the same as the encoder block, plus one extra sublayer.

Where an encoder block was constructed of two sublayers - 1) self-attention, 2) feed-forward, the decoder block has the extra sublayer for cross-attention. So it looks like:

  1. Masked multi-head self-attention. The decoder attending to its own tokens so far, with the causal mask so no position sees the future.
  2. Cross-attention with the encoder output. The decoder attending to the encoder’s output, the step that finally connects the two halves.
  3. The feed-forward network. Identical to the encoder, we end with a feedforward network to finally transform the result.

Additionally, each of these operations is wrapped in the same normalization and residual adding as the encoder before. So for each sublayer, we normalize, go through the sublayer, and add the un-normalized input back.

Putting it all together, this looks like:

4.4.1 A Decoder Block, in Code

Now, let’s write the code for what this decoder block looks like when we put it all together. You’ll notice it’s very similar to the encoder block we put together in the last section.

class DecoderBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, heads, d_ff, dropout=0.1):
        super(DecoderBlock, self).__init__()
        self.attention       = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, heads)   # masked self-attention
        self.cross_attention = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, heads)   # cross-attention (its own, separate weights)
        self.feed_forward    = FeedForward(d_model, d_ff)
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.norm3 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.dropout1 = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.dropout2 = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.dropout3 = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, X, enc_out, src_mask, trg_mask):
        # Sublayer 1: MASKED self-attention - Q, K, V all from the decoder's own input
        norm_X = self.norm1(X)
        self_attn = self.attention(norm_X, norm_X, norm_X, mask=trg_mask)
        X_1 = X + self.dropout1(self_attn)

        # Sublayer 2: cross-attention - Q from the decoder, K & V from the encoder output
        norm_X_1 = self.norm2(X_1)
        cross_attn = self.cross_attention(enc_out, enc_out, norm_X_1, mask=src_mask)
        X_2 = X_1 + self.dropout2(cross_attn)

        # Sublayer 3: position-wise feed-forward network
        norm_X_2 = self.norm3(X_2)
        ff_output = self.feed_forward(norm_X_2)
        X_3 = X_2 + self.dropout3(ff_output)

        return X_3

The differences from the encoder block are really just:

  1. Two separate attention objects. self.attention and self.cross_attention are both MultiHeadAttention, but different objects so each carries its own independent W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O.

  2. forward takes four inputs, not one. The encoder block only needed X. The decoder block also needs:

  • enc_out: the encoder’s output for cross-attention
  • trg_mask: The causal triangular mask for self-attention
  • src_mask: a mask we actually DO sometimes need in cross-attention to hide padding for different sequence lengths in batches. We’ll talk about this more later as it only matters for batching, which we haven’t yet covered.
  1. The extra sublayer. Sublayer 2, which is cross-attention, has one extra thing worth pointing out. We normalize X_1, which is the decoder’s current running representation, and give that as the query. We don’t re-normalize enc_out, which becomes K and V, since this is exactly as it was produced, normalized, then held fixed from the encoder side.

As with the encoder block, we have a residual connection add the input back after every sublayer. So, putting that all together, the decoder comes together to look like:

4.5 The Decoder’s Role

We started this section by talking about how the role of the decoder is to autoregressively generate the next token, one at a time. But, actually nothing in the decoder block that we’ve talked about so far really does that. So how, actually, does that little dotted arrow that “runs until <eos>” actually operate? Where would I possibly get the next token from?

The answer is that, despite our “high-level” graphic showing: \[ \text{Input} → \text{Encoder} → \text{Decoder} → \text{Output} \]

as four very distinct blocks, the relation between \(\text{Decoder}\) and \(\text{Output}\) is where that clean pipeline starts to break down a bit.

The decoder’s role is, generally, to generate the next token. But in isolation the decoder stack is actually still an understanding sort of stack - meant to prepare us to generate the next token. It’s not like all of a sudden the same attention mechanisms and feed-forward networks are now doing generation simply because they exist in a decoder block - how they’re used has to be to help with generation rather than to help purely with understanding.

And indeed, everything we’ve built so far - and the decoder block if it sits entirely on its own - still only turns vectors into vectors. \(X_{out}\) is an \(n_{\text{out}} × d_{\text{model}}\) matrix - exactly the same kind of representation the encoder produced, now just relating the words that exist so far in the output to each other via self-attention, and the input via cross-attention. The decoder doesn’t actually produce a token yet. What we have been calling the “output” is what produces the token.

We’re going to get to that next. The important part to understand for the decoder’s role is that it’s fundamentally tied to the output in a way that the input and the encoder weren’t. Getting the input is work you do once. Similarly, getting the encoder’s representation of the input is work you do once.

The decoder, instead, runs repeatedly on a growing sequence, where its result is fed into the output layer to get an actual next token, that next token is appended to the existing sequence, and that becomes the input to run through the decoder again.

The decoder’s role is to “generate” insofar as its role is to produce a rich, highly contextualized representation of the output so far, that informs what the next token will be, but is not literally yet what the next token will be.

So the two run in tandem, over and over again.

\[ 1. X_{\text{output}} = [\text{<bos>}] \rightarrow DECODER \rightarrow X_{\text{out}} = \begin{bmatrix}{x_1 \ x_2 \ ... \ x_n}\end{bmatrix} \rightarrow OUTPUT \rightarrow ["\text{I}"] \\ \] \[ 2. X_{\text{output}} = [\text{<bos>}, \text{I}] \rightarrow DECODER \rightarrow X_{\text{out}} = \begin{bmatrix}{x_1 \ x_2 \ ... \ x_n \\ y_1 \ y_2 \ ... \ y_n}\end{bmatrix} \rightarrow OUTPUT \rightarrow ["\text{love}"] \\ \] \[ 3. X_{\text{output}} = [\text{<bos>}, \text{I}, \text{love}] \rightarrow DECODER \rightarrow X_{\text{out}} = \begin{bmatrix}{x_1 \ x_2 \ ... \ x_n \\ y_1 \ y_2 \ ... \ y_n \\ z_1 \ z_2 \ ... \ z_n}\end{bmatrix} \rightarrow OUTPUT \rightarrow ["\text{cats}"] \]

Then, that output is the final missing piece we need to discuss.

5. The Output

So, the final job we have to do is to turn an \(X_{out}\), and a growing one at that, which is coming out of the decoder, into a final prediction on a next token.

This is the job for the output layer, which fortunately, is by far the simplest portion of the entire architecture.

5.1 From Vector to Vocabulary

When we get \(X_\text{out}\) from the decoder, it’s still just representations of the current words in the sequence. It’s a size \(n_{\text{seq}} \times d_{\text{model}}\) matrix that says, “For every single word in the sequence so far, here’s a rich, vector representation of it, contextualized by all the other words so far, and the input we ran through the encoder”.

To turn that representation into a word, we need to somehow get to a score for every token in the vocabulary. Basically, if we want to pick the next word, we need to ask, “well, how likely is it that this is the next word?”, for every single word that we know.

Fortunately, that can just be done with the simplest type of layer we know in deep learning: the simple linear projection.

self.output_projection = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab_size)

This layer takes our current representation, and multiplies it by a set of learnable weights that transform that output to represent a prediction for each word in the vocabulary.

Applied to \(X_\text{out}\), it maps each row’s \(d_\text{model}\) vector to a \(\text{vocab\_size}\) vector (plus the batch dimension in code, as always):

logits = self.output_projection(X_out)   # (n_out, d_model) -> (n_out, vocab_size)

Each row coming out of this is a set of logits. A raw, unnormalized score per vocabulary token.

Of course, a softmax can turn each set of logits into a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary:

\[P(\text{next token}) = \text{softmax}(\text{logits})\]

So we get, for every token in our vocabulary, a probability that that token should be the next one in the sequence.

5.2 Which Row to Use

Of course, as we just said, the projection produces a distribution for every row. And every row represents a word in the current sequence, which grows every time we add a new word. So we end up with a vector of probabilities for the next token, for every single word in the sequence. Which one do we use?

The answer is that at generation time, we only read the last row - and determine the next word based on the next token that the final row in the decoder’s output representation represents.

This might be confusing. The key thing is to think about each row at position \(i\) predicting what the token at position \(i+1\) will be. With [<bos>, I, love] fed in, row 1 corresponds to <bos> and predicts what will be in position 2. This ends up being “I” at row 2. Now row 2 predicts what’s at position 3, and row 3 will predict what’s at position 4. Each row in the output is predicting what the token in the next position will be, so once we use the output at row 2 to get row 3, we don’t need it anymore. It tells us about a token we’ve already decided.

📌 Note: But we don’t have to just interpret it that way - it’s a mathematical truth that the last row, the new one that runs through the decoder, is actually all that is going to be different in the final output. So this means it’s not only the correct one to use, but that actually this is something that can be exploited at generation time to speed things up, with something called a KV Cache. Read Appendix 4 for more details!

5.3 How to Use a Probability Distribution of Tokens

Let’s say that the sequence so far is:

\[ \text{She poured water from the pitcher into the glass until it was \_\_\_} \]

You probably want the next token prediction to be “full”, or at least, to be likely to be “full”. You probably also want it to be likely to say “filled”. You probably don’t want it to say “potato”.

As it turns out, getting a probability distribution, over all tokens in the vocabulary, is quite an important concept for a task such as language modeling, where there are certainly “more right” and “more wrong” answers, but not necessarily always “perfect” answers you’d want every single time. The output is more important than just predicting one token, it’s useful because a good distribution gives us a good idea of how well every possible word fits, and thus lets us choose one with a little flexibility.

5.3.1 A Theoretical Distribution

The final output we get ends up being a probability distribution over all possible tokens. It might look something like this:

mpl.rcParams['font.family'] = 'DejaVu Sans'
TEXT = '#2b2b2b'

# A plausible next-token distribution for:
# "She poured water from the pitcher into the glass until it was ___"
tokens = ['full', 'filled', 'overflowing', 'nearly', 'empty', 'yellow', 'potato']
probs  = [0.54,   0.17,     0.1,          0.065,     0.03,    0.01,  0.001]

BLUE, ORANGE = '#A9CCE3', '#F5CBA7'          # sensible words vs. the nonsense one
colors = [BLUE]*(len(tokens)-1) + [ORANGE]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
y = range(len(tokens))
ax.barh(y, probs, color=colors, edgecolor='#5b5b5b', linewidth=0.6)
ax.set_yticks(list(y)); ax.set_yticklabels(tokens, fontsize=12, color=TEXT)
ax.invert_yaxis()

for i, p in enumerate(probs):
    ax.text(p + 0.006, i, f'{p:.2f}' if p >= 0.01 else '≈ 0',
            va='center', fontsize=10.5, color=TEXT)

ax.set_xlim(0, 0.52)
ax.set_xlabel('probability the model assigns to this next token', fontsize=11, color=TEXT)
for s in ['top', 'right']: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
for s in ['left', 'bottom']: ax.spines[s].set_color('#bdbdbd')
ax.tick_params(colors=TEXT)
ax.grid(axis='x', color='#e8e8e8', linewidth=0.8); ax.set_axisbelow(True)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Since it’s a probability distribution, the values must sum to 1 (over the whole vocabulary - here assume we only show the top choices). This means we’ll have words that are very likely, words that are less likely, and words that are very unlikely.

5.3.2 Sampling the Distribution

A good token distribution is likely peaked, but not spiked. Here, “full” is the clear favorite, but there are other genuinely reasonable words that carry a decent amount of probability as well. Only truly nonsensical things should sit at essentially zero.

The simplest way to turn a distribution like this into a literal choice of next token would be to just take the most likely token every time. This is called greedy decoding. You’d simply do:

next_token_logits = logits[-1]                 # last row only
next_token = torch.argmax(next_token_logits)   # the single most likely token

But, importantly, greedy decoding isn’t the only option. We could also do sampling, which works well precisely because we expect to get a good distribution out. If the probability mass sits on reasonable words, we can afford to not always choose the single most likely thing, and the result will still make sense. And indeed, this is more in line with how language works. In the above example, both “full” and “filled” are completely reasonable things to say - they don’t even change the meaning. Both are a good choice, so sampling sometimes one, sometimes the other, is a genuine reflection of how language can be used in many different ways, even still to convey the exact same meaning.

If we do our sampling in proportion to the probabilities, we’ll usually get “full”, but sometimes get “filled” or “overflowing”. We will still basically never get “potato”. That’s how we give generated text variety without letting it stray too far or become incoherent. A good distribution is what makes non-greedy decoding safe. To sample the distribution, we’d instead do something like:

# sampling instead of greedy
probs = torch.softmax(logits[-1], dim=-1)
next_token = torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=1)

This is what the temperature that you’ve probably heard of refers to. It scales the logits before the softmax, so that lower temperature sharpens the distribution toward the top token and higher temperature flattens it to allow more variety. Then when you sample, you’re more or less likely to spread out from the “best” next token. We won’t heavily tune or explore temperature here, but understand that this is exactly where that knob comes into play.

One more decoding strategy worth knowing, because it’s what the original paper actually used, is beam search. Greedy decoding and sampling both commit to one token at a time, which can be short-sighted. The single most likely next token can lead into a sentence that ends up less likely overall than one that started with the runner-up. So in beam search, instead of keeping one sequence, you keep the top \(k\) partial sequences (the “beam”). At each step, you try extending every one of them by every possible next token, then score each candidate by its total log-probability so far, and keeps only the best \(k\) to continue.

When it’s done, it returns the best complete sequence. Though, since every token you add brings in another negative log-probability, this scoring naturally favors shorter outputs. To fix this, a length penalty is usually added to even that out. Beam search works well for tasks like translation, where there’s essentially one right answer and you want the most likely one. But it’s rarely used for open-ended generation, like chatbots, because chasing the single most probable sequence tends to produce bland, repetitive text, and that’s exactly where the variety from sampling helps.

So there are many options, and the best one depends on the task. For the simple date translation task we’ll have, where there’s only one correct output and the model will be very confident, plain greedy decoding is a great choice, and the one we’ll go with.

5.4 The Input-Output Connection

Before we talk about what the full assembly of all of this looks like, there’s a couple more things to be clear about in how outputs become inputs, which is the loop that the decoder is constantly running. What does the output feeding back into the decoder actually look like?

5.4.1 What to do With New Tokens

So, we’ve chosen the next token. Now, we stick it onto the sequence. But there’s a few more nuances to talk about before this loop is really fully complete.

First, let’s talk about what we do with a token. That final output gives us a token ID - a single integer which is the index of the winning word in the vocabulary. The decoder, of course, can’t just take a token ID. Like every other transformer block, it expects embeddings. So before this new token can re-enter the loop, it has to become a vector again.

We do this, of course, by re-embedding it. The key thing here is that we do it with the same input embedding layer we used for every other token. The chosen token ID goes through the full process that any of our original “input” ids went through: the token-embedding lookup, adding the positional encoding for its position, and becoming a \(d_\text{model}\) vector. Then, we can append it as the new final row of the decoder’s input. Then the whole (now one longer) sequence can run through the stack again.

So every new token that’s generated by the decoder is generated from just a regular input embedding of the whole sequence so far - we don’t keep anything from the decoder stack to “inform” that token in any kind of a special way. (Conceptually, at least - a reader coming off Appendix 4 will note that we do store some information for computation’s sake, but in a way that’s computationally equivalent to a fresh pass.) So at least from an information standpoint, the pass that makes the next token is an independent pass through the full decoder.

Putting it all together now, understanding the job of the output, we see a complete view of how this comes together into a pipeline:

5.4.2 The Relation Between Input and Output Layers

One more thing, is that there’s a symmetry between the input and output layers that we haven’t fully appreciated yet. Look at the two ends of the model:

  • the input embedding takes a token ID and produces a vector,
  • the output projection takes a vector and produces scores over token IDs.

They’re mirror images. Where one’s job is to turn a word into a vector, the other’s is to turn a vector back into a word. And in fact, because a word should mean the same thing whether it’s going in through the embedding or being chosen on the way out, it makes sense for the two to be sort of “opposites” of one another.

In fact, they’re so closely related that many models explicitly tie them - the original Transformer included. Tying then just means the output projection literally is the embedding matrix, transposed: the logit for each token is just the dot product between the decoder’s final vector and that token’s embedding. In other words, the model predicts whichever token’s embedding points most nearly the same direction as what it computed. This takes advantage of the same “direction means meaning” idea from our word embeddings. The main benefit is efficiency: the embedding matrix of a 100k-token vocabulary is huge, and tying means storing it once. But the two jobs aren’t perfectly identical, and many large modern models opt keep them separate to allow them to be as different as they need be. For the tiny vocabulary we’ll have for our task and model in this notebook, the difference is negligible, so we’ll keep them as two separate layers.

6. Assembling the Full Transformer

We’ve now built every individual piece of the core transformer architecture:

  1. the input pipeline that turns text into vectors
  2. the encoder with its all-knowing multi-head attention
  3. the decoder with its masked attention and cross attention to the encoder
  4. the output that turns a vector back into a token

Each component, on its own, we understand in detail. And even (most of) how they come together. But of course, when assembling all of this into a full, final pipeline, there are a few extra things to consider, in how exactly those arrows between these segments are passing information.

So in this section, we’ll talk about those first. And then go ahead and proceed with our complete assembled transformer, that we can actually try to train.

6.1 The Input to the Encoder vs. to the Decoder

Hopefully by now, you’ve come to understand why our initial, simplified architecture is actually probably better drawn like this:

And there’s something that we need to discuss a little bit more before we go on, and that’s what I’ve labeled in this diagram as Input 2.

In the last 2 sections, when we were talking about how we append the next token back to the input and feed it through again, we talked about how that means re-embedding it and adding back its positional encoding. But we didn’t answer the question: embedding it with what embedding layer?

Well, we already have the input pipeline for the encoder. Except it’s not necessarily true that we can re-use that same pipeline for our decoder step. And actually, in many cases, like the French-to-English example we keep referencing, we can’t.

The reason and decision really comes down to if your input and output share the same vocabulary. In a case like French-to-English translation, the encoder needs to understand the French input sequence, while the decoder needs to understand a growing English sequence. The languages share letters, sure, but tokenization as we’ve come to understand it will not apply to both in the same way. Nor would the same tokens come to mean the same thing, even if we could share them (“chat” in French vs “chat” in English mean very different things).

But nothing really requires it be separate, either. Imagine the task of summarization: the input is a long article and the output is a short summary of it, both in English. The two are completely different sequences, but they draw from the same vocabulary. An encoder-decoder is a great fit for the task, where the encoder reads and fully understands the whole article, and the decoder generates the summary conditioned on that understanding. But since the source and target share a vocabulary, the input pipeline that prepares text for the encoder can be re-used for the decoder just fine.

In fact, in the small task we’re about to train on (translating a date from one format into another), we will re-use the exact same input. Our input and output will both be made of digits, letters, and some common symbols, so they’ll share a single vocabulary. That means that when we assemble the model, we can use one embedding for both the input into the encoder and the input into the decoder, rather than the two separate ones like a French-to-English model would need.

6.2 The Other Mask

Back when we first wrote our DecoderBlock implementation, we gave it two different mask arguments in the forward call - the causal trg_mask for masked self-attention, and a src_mask that we said for cross-attention but otherwise left almost entirely unexplained. All we said was that it was “a mask we sometimes need to hide padding,” and that we’d come back to it later. Well, now is later.

6.2.1 When to Use the src_mask

The reason that we waited until now to talk about it, is that this is another one of those training time / data organization nuances, not really a critical feature of the architecture. If you only ever ran through one sequence at a time, as we’ve mostly thought of, we wouldn’t need it at all. But in practice, especially during training time, we process many sequences at once - as a batch.

Of course, a tensor has to be rectangular, meaning every sequence in the batch must be the same length. In basically any real application, that won’t be the case. There are specific cases where it wouldn’t be necessary at all, like if we were translating dates in the reverse from what we’ll actually do - from a fixed format (like 2026-06-05) to their full format (June 5th, 2026). If all input sequences were always exactly the same length, we’d never need a src_mask, so it is situational. It’s just that in most real situations, inputs will have mis-matched lengths. And to fix mis-matched lengths, we pad the shorter ones, tacking on a special <pad> token, over and over, until each sequence reaches the length of the longest in the batch.

But padding tokens aren’t tokens we want to affect anything - i.e, we don’t want attention on them. So we need to ignore them, much like we do in masked self-attention, with a mask of their own.

So the mask mechanism is the same, the one we already know well from the triangular mask in masked self-attention.

  • We mark which positions are padding and set their attention scores to −∞
  • We do it before the softmax so they get zero weight

The difference is just how we construct it.

  • the causal mask, because it depends only on sequence length, is baked into the architecture. The decoder must act autoregressively no matter what data you feed it.
  • the padding mask, because it depends entirely on the data (which positions happened to be padding in this batch), has to be constructed for the specific batch.

This padding mask is still passed into the MultiHeadAttention calculation. But it’s coming from the source sequence that gets padded on the encoder side, so the source padding mask (src_mask) is needed anywhere the source is attended to. That means that we need it in:

  • the encoder’s self-attention to make sure source tokens don’t attend to source padding
  • the decoder’s cross-attention to make sure the decoder doesn’t attend to source padding that was used in the encoder.

You might wonder: we batch the target sequences too, so they get padded as well. Won’t that mean the decoder’s self-attention needs to mask that target padding too?

And fortunately, it’s already handled for free by the causal mask. Since we always pad at the end of a sequence, the padding is always “in the future.” And the causal mask already handles masking out the future. So a real target token never reaches the padding. The causal mask, which we added for a totally different reason (autoregression), also happens to totally take care of this issue.

(One thing, the pad positions themselves will still compute outputs, just junk, since they do attend back to real tokens. But when it comes time to calculate the loss, we can just ignore those positions. We can let them generate and be whatever, we know we aren’t going to actually use them in the end anyway.)

6.2.2 Seeing a Real Example

We’ve said that the mask operates just the same as the causal mask, it’s just not triangular. But it’s the exact same idea: just 1’s and 0’s for “attention is allowed” vs “attention is not allowed”. And constructing it is super simple: all we need to know is what we padded.

Say a batch has two source sequences of different lengths:

  • “le chat dort” → [le, chat, dort] (3 tokens)
  • “il pleut” → [il, pleut] (2 tokens)

To batch them, we pad the shorter up to length 3:

[ le,  chat,  dort  ]
[ il,  pleut, <pad> ]

Then the src_mask just records which positions are real (1), and which are padding (0):

[ 1, 1, 1 ]
[ 1, 1, 0 ]

After that, all of the same advantages of masking apply and are handled exactly the same as the causal mask.

This is also why, though we’d need it for differing sequence lengths in a batch, we can’t make it ahead of time. We only know what our batches will look like during training. And for that reason, a padding mask is also just a training-time necessity. At generation time, running one sequence, there’s nothing to pad and nothing to mask.

But actually building it requires knowing exactly what the data looks like, so we’ll revisit the concept one more time when we get to actually setting up training. The example task that we’re going to use will be training on a date-format translation task, except unlike the exception I pointed out above, our inputs will be variable lengths, and so we will need to handle this padding. But more on that when we get there!

6.3 The Full Model in Code

Ok, done with the few extra nuances, it’s time to write the thing! We have already built many of these parts as we’ve gone along. Actual assembly is now mostly just plumbing, writing four classes that each handle a major component, arranging all of the pieces to come together into a real working model. Those major parts will be:

  1. an Input - this will cover the source input pipeline (embedding + positional encoding)
  2. an Encoder - will first use the input, followed by N stacked EncoderBlocks,
  3. a Decoder - this will include the same input pipeline, followed by N stacked DecoderBlocks,
  4. a Transformer will put the two pieces together, and handle the few extra outstanding things. It will be the wrapper that holds both encoder and decoder, handles building the masks, runs the source through the encoder and the target through the decoder, and applies the output projection.

We’ll build them in that order.

6.3.1 The Input

First, we create an InputEmbedding layer as its own thing. This is the general case - we can either call this same layer in both the Encoder and Decoder parts to have them explicitly share their embedding layer, OR we could call two separate instances of this if we didn’t want them to share.

In our case, with the shared vocabulary, we want to use this same input twice. But in the French-English translation example, you would make two separate instances of this. It’s all up to what task your architecture is meant for.

The code itself will reuse all of the pieces we already built back in Section 1. So this code is just a small wrapper that takes token IDs, looks up their embeddings, adds positional encodings, and applies dropout.

class InputEmbedding(nn.Module):
    """The 'Input' block from the diagram: token IDs -> vectors + positional encodings."""
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, d_model, max_len, dropout=0.1):
        super(InputEmbedding, self).__init__()
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)
        pe = torch.tensor(get_positional_encodings(max_len, d_model), dtype=torch.float)
        self.register_buffer("pos_encoding", pe) # store the positional encodings
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, x):                       # x: token IDs, (N, seq_len)
        seq_len = x.shape[1]
        x = self.embedding(x) + self.pos_encoding[:seq_len] # add the fixed PE to the embedding
        return self.dropout(x) # dropout at the END - right before the next layer

A few things to point out here:

  • The positional-encoding function is implemented here with the get_positional_encodings that we wrote before, but stored with register_buffer. This makes it a part of the module - moved to the GPU and stored there alongside it without being a learnable parameter, since sinusoidal positional encodings have nothing to learn.

  • nn.Embedding is a torch built-in layer, like the nn.Linear we discussed before. This special kind of layer is exactly the lookup table we described back when we first talked about embeddings. It contains a learnable weight matrix of shape \(n_{\text{vocab}} \times d_{\text{model}}\), with one row per token in the vocabulary, that returns row \(i\) for a token index \(i\). It does the exact same thing as the “one-hot vector times the embedding matrix” calculation that we talked about in Section 1, just done as a direct row-lookup instead of an actual matrix multiply. The nn.Embedding layer is a special layer that knows to do this instead of the full matrix multiply.

  • nn.Dropout is slipped into here again, just like we did with every encoder and decoder block so far. It might be obvious why dropping random activations helps the model from over-relying on certain features, but dropping parts of an embedding might seem like a stranger choice. But it’s still for the exact same reason. Regularizing here means that the next layer, the first layer of the encoder or decoder, doesn’t get every single feature of the embedding vector, and thus can’t learn to over-rely on certain features of that vector.

6.3.2 The Encoder

Next, we’ll assemble the encoder. But first, actually, we need to rewrite our original EncoderBlock code. At the time that we wrote that code, we didn’t yet understand the need for masking, and so we left it out. Now that we’ve covered the role of the source mask, we need to just make a tiny edit to that code to be sure that it can take in and handle that.

The two line changes are pointed out with comments.

class EncoderBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, heads, d_ff, dropout=0.1):
        super(EncoderBlock, self).__init__()
        self.attention = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, heads)
        self.feed_forward = FeedForward(d_model, d_ff)
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.dropout1 = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.dropout2 = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, X, mask=None):                                   # <- added mask=None by default
        norm_X = self.norm1(X)
        attention_output = self.attention(norm_X, norm_X, norm_X, mask=mask)  # <- attention is already wired for a mask, but pass it through here
        X_1 = X + self.dropout1(attention_output)

        norm_X_1 = self.norm2(X_1)
        ff_output = self.feed_forward(norm_X_1)
        X_2 = X_1 + self.dropout2(ff_output)
        return X_2

Then, building up the encoder is just a few lines, since it just means stacking encoder blocks, which contain all of the relevant operations, on top of each other.

class Encoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, num_layers, heads, d_ff, dropout=0.1):
        super(Encoder, self).__init__()
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList(
            [EncoderBlock(d_model, heads, d_ff, dropout) for _ in range(num_layers)]
        )
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)       # <- new addition: final LayerNorm (needed with pre-norm)

    def forward(self, x, mask):                 # x: (N, src_len, d_model), already embedded
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x, mask)
        return self.norm(x)                     # <- normalize once more on the way out

So as you can see, really all this does is just puts num_layers encoder blocks all in a row. Just a few things to point out:

  • nn.ModuleList is a new piece of PyTorch. It’s meant for cases exactly like stacking our already made encoder modules: it’s really just a list that holds sub-modules, but unlike a regular Python list, everything gets registered with PyTorch so all weights are properly tracked, and will show up in model.parameters(). It just tells PyTorch “here’s a bunch of trainable things”.

  • We do wrap it around a “normal” list, with the list comprehension: python [EncoderBlock(...) for _ in range(num_layers)] simply making num_layers separate EncoderBlock objects. Since each is a distinct object, it’ll have its own \(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O\) and \(W_{\text{ff}}\) weights.

  • In forward, the loop is where the “stacked” behavior really comes to fruition. We go through each layer in that list, run x through it, take the x that comes out of it, and put it into the next one. The same mask is handed to every block, because the same batch passes through all blocks to get the final output.

  • Remember here that the first x is going to arrive already embedded. We’ll see when we build the full transformer object.

  • num_layers is the stack depth N, a hyperparameter - the original transformer used 6; we’ll pick something small for our toy task.

  • We snuck in an “extra” nn.LayerNorm. Remember that with pre-norm, each sublayer normalizes its input, but the residual stream that runs through the whole stack never gets normalized itself - it’s just added onto, block after block. So the last block hands back an un-normalized \(x\). This would leave one “missing” at the end - our final encoder output wouldn’t be normalized, if we didn’t add one more norm to the end.

6.3.3 The Decoder

The Decoder structurally matches the encoder almost exactly - a lot of the work already went into building our DecoderBlock object back in the Decoder Section, so now all that’s left is stacking a bunch of them together.

class Decoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, num_layers, heads, d_ff, dropout=0.1):
        super(Decoder, self).__init__()
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList(
            [DecoderBlock(d_model, heads, d_ff, dropout) for _ in range(num_layers)]
        )
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)

    def forward(self, x, enc_out, src_mask, trg_mask):   # x: (N, trg_len, d_model), already embedded
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x, enc_out, src_mask, trg_mask)
        return self.norm(x)

So what is different from the encoder?

  • It stacks DecoderBlocks instead of EncoderBlock’s, of course.

  • forward must take four arguments instead of two, for the same reasons that our DecoderBlock’s forward needed 4 arguments. On top of x (the target sequence, already embedded), it also receives:

    • enc_out - the encoder’s output.
    • src_mask - the mask for the encoder output, for handling padding of different sequence lengths, and
    • trg_mask - the causal mask to block the future.

    These masks will get defined in the Transformer object.

  • Just like the encoder, we loop through the layers in the forward definition. Same as the encoder, x changes from one block to the next. But those extra inputs: enc_out, src_mask, and trg_mask stay fixed, handed identically to every block.

  • Also just like the encoder, we end with a nn.LayerNorm on the output, because pre-norm doesn’t normalize the final output as-is.

So structurally, they’re really the same, and the differences just come down to how we had to construct the encoder vs decoder block differently, which we already covered extensively.

6.3.4 The Full Transformer

Now, finally, we really put it all together.

class Transformer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, d_model, num_layers, heads, d_ff, max_len,
                 src_pad_idx, trg_pad_idx, dropout=0.1):
        super(Transformer, self).__init__()
        # Define all of the sections we just made
        self.input_embedding = InputEmbedding(vocab_size, d_model, max_len, dropout)
        #ONE Input block, that we'll share since our source and target share a vocabulary. Otherwise, we'd define two here!
        self.encoder = Encoder(d_model, num_layers, heads, d_ff, dropout)
        self.decoder = Decoder(d_model, num_layers, heads, d_ff, dropout)
        self.output_projection = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab_size)   # the "Output" / prediction layer is so simple, it just gets defined right here
        self.src_pad_idx = src_pad_idx # padding for the SOURCE - input
        self.trg_pad_idx = trg_pad_idx # padding for the TARGET - output

    def make_src_mask(self, src):
        # 1 where the token is real, 0 where it's padding
        # shape (N, 1, 1, src_len) so it broadcasts over heads and query positions
        # we get this DIRECTLY from the source padding!
        return (src != self.src_pad_idx).unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(2)

    def make_trg_mask(self, trg):
        N, trg_len = trg.shape
        # lower-triangular causal mask, shape (N, 1, trg_len, trg_len)
        trg_mask = torch.tril(torch.ones((trg_len, trg_len), device=trg.device))
        return trg_mask.expand(N, 1, trg_len, trg_len)

    def forward(self, src, trg):
        # 1) build the masks
        src_mask = self.make_src_mask(src)       # (N, 1, 1, src_len)
        trg_mask = self.make_trg_mask(trg)       # (N, 1, trg_len, trg_len)

        # 2) embed both inputs, with the SAME embedding object
        src_emb = self.input_embedding(src)      # (N, src_len, d_model) for the input (source)
        trg_emb = self.input_embedding(trg)      # (N, trg_len, d_model) for the output (target)

        # 3) pass through the encoder
        enc_out = self.encoder(src_emb, src_mask)                     # X_enc: (N, src_len, d_model)

        # 4) pass through the decoder
        dec_out = self.decoder(trg_emb, enc_out, src_mask, trg_mask)  # X_out: (N, trg_len, d_model)

        logits = self.output_projection(dec_out)  # (N, trg_len, vocab_size)
        return logits

All things considered, it’s relatively brief. And of course that’s one of the big advantages to building up these building blocks as their own objects. Now that we have a full encoder, we just have to say “go through the encoder” - we can look to that specific object for the encoder architecture.

The forward pass is the entire architecture - the full flow of an input through the entire process, so let’s make sure we understand every line there to see how everything we’ve talked about finally comes together.

📌 Note: Recall in the above code, and what we’re about to discuss that \(N\) is referring to batch size. Where before we’ve talked about “N” layers in the encoder/decoder stacks, in code, that has become num_layers to be more explicit.

The main components to this forward pass are:

  1. The first thing we do is build the masks.
  • make_trg_mask is the causal torch.tril which simply constructs a triangular mask from the target length. Remember that this kind of triangular mask, and the size it needs to be, is just exactly determined by what the current sequence length is, so this needs no other information than “what is the current target sequence”.
  • make_src_mask is the padding mask we make from the source. Remember that, similarly, this mask just needs to assign a 1 where a real token was placed, and 0 where a padding token was placed. So this also needs no extra information other than what the current source is - it marks which source positions are real (src != pad_idx), and it’s shaped to broadcast across heads and query positions so a single mask covers the whole score matrix. All that we’ll need to do is tell it what the padding token looks like, what its ID is, which we’ll pin down when we get to actually passing in data.
  1. Then, we embed the sequences with the same InputEmbedding object. Both self.input_embedding(src) and self.input_embedding(trg) call the same object, because as we discussed, in this case, the vocabulary is shared - with tokens always meaning the same thing on both sides. After embedding, both come out as (N, seq_len, d_model).
  2. We run the full encoder first. It gives us enc_out, which is what we’ve been calling X_enc - the fixed, fully contextualized output from the encoder, that we hold fixed after the forward pass and use in the decoder. Its shape coming out is (N, src_len, d_model). It’s computed once, then handed to the decoder in the next step.
  3. The decoder runs after, using that enc_out. This gives us dec_out, which is what we’ve been calling X_out, the contextualized target representation that we use to get the next token. It has shape (N, trg_len, d_model).
  4. The output projection picks the next token. Finally, we give that X_out to the output layer, which projects each position from d_model up to vocab_size, giving logits of shape (N, trg_len, vocab_size)

Then, even though we aren’t quite ready to train yet, we can put this together, and make sure that it all runs forward, giving back the correct shape, at least with dummy numbers:

# a small toy config
vocab_size = 15          # something small - e.g. digits, '-', eos, bos, pad, unk
d_model, num_layers, heads, d_ff, max_len = 64, 3, 4, 256, 32
src_pad_idx = trg_pad_idx = 0

model = Transformer(vocab_size, d_model, num_layers, heads, d_ff, max_len,
                    src_pad_idx, trg_pad_idx)

N, src_len, trg_len = 2, 18, 11       # batch of 2; a padded source, a target
src = torch.randint(1, vocab_size, (N, src_len))   # fake token IDs
trg = torch.randint(1, vocab_size, (N, trg_len))

logits = model(src, trg)
print("src:   ", tuple(src.shape))
print("trg:   ", tuple(trg.shape))
print("logits:", tuple(logits.shape))
src:    (2, 18)
trg:    (2, 11)
logits: (2, 11, 15)

7. Training the Transformer

So we’ve done the full assembling - we literally have the Transformer defined. But looking at the forward, a few things probably feel conspicuously absent. Some of these are things we’ll cover right now: how to make sure that our targets really only learn from positions they should be able to see, what signal actually determines if we’re getting the answer right or wrong, the actual learning of the weights, and how to do it all when data comes in as a batch.

Other things that we had discussed - like the autoregressive loop that produces one token at a time, appends it, and feeds it back in - will come down to how we use the model, after it’s trained. We’ll cover those as their own set of topics, in Section 9, once we’ve trained this model on a real task in Section 8.

So this Section is just all about the theory and practicalities of training. We have a full Transformer architecture, we can pass in a tensor, it’ll get multiplied by all of the weights, and we get a set of logits back out. How, then, do we set it up with data so those weights shift to produce correct outputs? How do we measure correctness? How do we know how much to change the model by? These are all training time considerations.

7.1 Teacher Forcing

The first important concept that we need because things are different at training time vs. at generation time is something called teacher forcing. Basically, it’s how we mimic autoregressive generation - making just one token at a time, conditioned by what comes before - when during training, we actually already have the whole answer.

7.1.1 The Core Idea

Maybe the most obvious way to train a model that wants to run autoregressively is to train it autoregressively: just give it the input, have it generate token 1, feed that back in to generate token 2, and so on, and every time you look at the correct answer and ask if it was right or wrong.

That would work, but it’s a bad idea and not done in practice for two huge reasons:

  1. Sequential generation like that is painfully slow. Generating the output one step at a time means doing an entire forward pass, through the whole big decoder, with a whole new pass per token. You can’t parallelize, run through whole batches at once, or take real good advantage of knowing what the whole sequence should be ahead of time.
  2. Early in training, the model is terrible. If you rely on what the model generates at step \(i\) to determine step \(i+1\), it’s likely to be wrong at \(i+1\) if it was wrong at \(i\). It will compound its own errors over the sequence and likely just produce garbage, especially early on. But as those errors compound, the model can struggle to even get started on actually good trajectories.

Teacher forcing fixes both. And the core idea is to exploit the feature that we’ve already mentioned here a few times: during training, you have an entire correct sequence, and you know what the next token should be given the truth so far at every step. Teacher forcing just does exactly this - instead of running the “real” autoregressive loop, where the model gets its own previously generated tokens back, we only ever give it the ground-truth for a given position. We say “what would you generate for j…. given this is what {a….i} actually was”. The teacher “forces” the correct history at every step.

And remember, this is actually the whole reason we built the causal mask! As we discussed in Section 4 and then proved in Appendix 4, causal masking keeps previous tokens in the sequence frozen, not allowing them to look ahead. We did this so that the current position we’re looking at is the only one that has “full access” to see everything. But if we trained autoregressively, where we pick off the last row to predict the next token anyway, then who cares if a previous position’s embedding changes - we’re only looking at the most recent one anyway. It’s precisely because we want to feed the model the entire target sequence at once, and see how every token position does with the true prefix, that we need the causal mask - it allows us to predict the next token at every position at once in a single parallel forward pass.

(I encourage you to visit Appendix 4 if you haven’t already and need to see this play out with the exact matrix math.
