[XX]     15 june 1912  ->  1992-06-15    (wanted 1912-06-15)
[XX]       15/06/1912  ->  1972-06-15    (wanted 1912-06-15)
[ok]     15 june 2088  ->  2088-06-15    (wanted 2088-06-15)
[ok]       15/06/2088  ->  2088-06-15    (wanted 2088-06-15)

So, this is interesting. We do ok for 2088 but not for 1912. What’s different?

Well, back to the slot table: in a 19xx year (hundreds = 9), the tens digit was always 5-9 in training. A 1 in the tens slot beside a 9 is a pairing the model never saw - and here it quietly “corrected” it to a 9, a tens value it has seen in the 1900s.

But it’s the exact same issue with 2088, and the model has no issue. For whatever reason, the model has stronger priors about what 19xx years are allowed than what 20xx years are (you could try out a few more dates, and find this is generally true).

One more thing to notice, is that in all cases, the last digit of the year copies faithfully. As we saw, this is the one slot that was always allowed to be any digit, so it makes sense that it would copy even when other parts of the year don’t.

2) A year with digits in slots they’ve never been in. Next, we’ll put digits in places they’ve never been. This asks something real: Did the model learn a clean, position-blind “copy these digits,” or did it just learn what years tend to look like?

Test cases: 1850 and 3017

We should expect a well generalized model to do this, but can’t be sure. We already saw it struggle with the last example, and this one is harder. We might expect 3017 to do worse than 1850 because the start digit is different, so the model’s immediate understanding is worse. But maybe, it’ll default back to the “copy-exact” behavior we’d hoped for when it doesn’t have all of its assumptions of a “19xx” year behind it.

test_probes = [
    ("15 june 1850", "1850-06-15"),  # unseen value, easier case (year still starts 1)
    ("15/06/1850", "1850-06-15"),
    ("15 june 3017", "3017-06-15"),  # same idea, harder (year starts 3)
    ("15/06/3017", "3017-06-15")
]

for human, expected in test_probes:
    got = generate(model, human)
    flag = "ok" if got == expected else "XX"
    print(f"[{flag}] {human:>16}  ->  {got:<12}  (wanted {expected})")
[XX]     15 june 1850  ->  1950-06-15    (wanted 1850-06-15)
[XX]       15/06/1850  ->  1950-06-15    (wanted 1850-06-15)
[XX]     15 june 3017  ->  2017-06-15    (wanted 3017-06-15)
[XX]       15/06/3017  ->  2017-06-15    (wanted 3017-06-15)

So years this far outside the range have fully broken it. The model changed 1850 → 1950 (the novel hundreds digit 8 snapped to 9), and 3017 → 2017 (the novel thousands digit 3 snapped to 2).

The model did not learn a position-blind “copy these digits.” It learned that the thousands slot is a 1 or 2 and the hundreds slot is a 0 or 9, and when you hand it a digit that violates that, it overrides the copy and substitutes the nearest value it has seen. The fact that both 3017 and 1850 fail completely suggests the thousands and hundreds priors are each absolute.

50 and 17 did copy though - so the model is consistent. It has no trouble copying the final 2 digits correctly if they’re what it thinks can follow the first 2. Once it “corrects” the first 2, those can copy as-is without issue.

3) A year that’s the wrong length - Years of course aren’t all 4 digits, but the model has never seen that. We’ll try what we know to be a valid year, sometime before 1000. This is a very different task - it doesn’t just go outside of values the model expects, but outside of the structure it’s come to expect as a pattern.

Test cases: 841 and 57

We can expect that this probably won’t work. The model even needs to decide on the behavior for this. Does the year in ISO format become “0841” or stay “841”? It likely won’t interpret “57” as the last 2 digits of the year, as a human might. Even then, the task could be interpreted ambiguously. We’ll mean here “the year 57”, but even a human might assume you meant, for instance, “1957” and are just referring to it as ’57.

test_probes = [
    ("15 june 841", "0841-06-15"),  # three digit year
    ("15/06/841", "0841-06-15"),
    ("15 june 57", "0057-06-15"),  # same idea, harder (2 digit year)
    ("15/06/57", "0057-06-15")
]

for human, expected in test_probes:
    got = generate(model, human)
    flag = "ok" if got == expected else "XX"
    print(f"[{flag}] {human:>16}  ->  {got:<12}  (wanted {expected})")
[XX]      15 june 841  ->  1981-06-15    (wanted 0841-06-15)
[XX]        15/06/841  ->  1981-06-15    (wanted 0841-06-15)
[XX]       15 june 57  ->  2057-06-15    (wanted 0057-06-15)
[XX]         15/06/57  ->  1977-06-15    (wanted 0057-06-15)

As expected, it simply can’t represent a year that isn’t four digits, so it forces one. We wanted “00”, but of course learned in the last example that the “19” or “20” starts are absolute - so of course we instead get a 19xx or 20xx year.

But notice that the numbers in our short years aren’t necessarily reliably appearing, either. In the last example, 57 becomes 1977 - not 1957 - and 841 becomes 1981. It seems, again, that the ones place - the only slot that got to see every number - is the only one that reliably copies into the correct place.

In both cases though, we’re off the edge of the structure entirely, and just grabbing for the nearest valid-looking year.

Put the three probes together and a precise picture emerges - one that maps almost exactly onto the slot table we built. The model learned to copy the year, but with a per-slot prior whose strength tracks how constrained that slot was in training:

  • The units slot saw every digit freely, so it copies anything, no questions asked.
  • The tens slot saw every digit but only in certain pairings, so it mostly copies but will occasionally “fix” a bad pairing (our 1912 and 2088 cases), though inconsistently.
  • The hundreds and thousands slots only ever saw two digits each, so the model treats that as law, snapping any novel digit back to a seen one every time.

So “does it generalize to an unseen year?” Not really. Or rather, only as far as each digit-slot’s training coverage allows. If the data had full coverage on a slot, it generalizes perfectly. If the data pinned a slot down to a small set, it treats that constraint as a rule and overrides the evidence in front of it to obey.

9.4.3 Case 2: A Convention It Was Never Told

In all of the Case 1 instances, we focused on changing the values the model had to handle. This, of course, does change its understanding, but we still gave it those new values within the same structure it came to expect. We can try instead, to probe structures it hasn’t seen before, to see if it learns, not just generally what to do with numbers, but some semblance of meaning.

When we made the data, we chose a few rigid formats. Those were:

INPUT FORMAT EXAMPLE
%d %B %Y 03 march 2019
%B %d, %Y march 03, 2019
%d %b %Y 03 mar 2019
%b %d %Y mar 03 2019
%A, %B %d, %Y sunday, march 03, 2019
%d/%m/%Y 03/03/2019 (always day/month/year)

For instance, dates that were given in the “/” convention assumed %d/%m/%Y - day, then month, then year. We chose one so that “03/04/1994” was clearly unambiguous - the model only ever saw that as day first. But it’s also very common for that same date “03/04/1994” to be month first. So we can push the boundaries of the conventions we had it learn, to see if some of them are more general.

1) Day and month swapped. The first thing we can do is to try that exact %d/%m/%Y with swaps for day and month.

Test cases: - 07/04/1994 and 07/15/1994

In the first case, the model will certainly give us back April 7, 1994 - 1994-04-07. It cannot possibly know that we might have meant “July 4, 1994”, and indeed no one could without knowing what convention we were using. The model, not knowing two conventions even exist, will surely give back the interpretation that’s well inside its distribution - that the data was DD/MM/YYYY.

The second case though, is more interesting. There is no 15th month. So it can’t give back an ISO date that actually exists if it follows its usual conventions. But we also can’t really reasonably expect it to somehow now know that MM/DD/YYYY is also a valid format. We’ll see what this produces, but it’s likely that, similar to above, if it’s a good copier of pieces into the right place (so long as it thinks the numbers can go in that slot), it might just give back 1994-15-07, as it probably makes more sense to assume the rule still follows, and just that 15 is valid in the second slot, than that the convention had flipped.

test_probes = [
    ("07/04/1994", "1994-04-07"),  # ambiguous DD/MM/YYYY format
    ("07/15/1994", "1994-07-15"),  # no 15th month, must be MM/DD/YYYY
]

for human, expected in test_probes:
    got = generate(model, human)
    flag = "ok" if got == expected else "XX"
    print(f"[{flag}] {human:>16}  ->  {got:<12}  (wanted {expected})")
[ok]       07/04/1994  ->  1994-04-07    (wanted 1994-04-07)
[XX]       07/15/1994  ->  1994-15-07    (wanted 1994-07-15)

Both exactly as predicted. 07/04/1994 → 1994-04-07: the model reads day-first, gives April 7th, and has no way to know we might have meant July 4th. This is it doing well on the task, exactly within its wheelhouse.

And 07/15/1994 → 1994-15-07 has the failure mode we saw coming. The model has no idea ‘15’ isn’t a valid month, so it follows the ordering rigidly and puts ‘15’ in the month slot. It’s not “choosing a convention”, it’s just following the rule, since that’s all it knows.

One detail worth flagging: here the model faithfully copied the out-of-range 15 into the month slot, rather than snapping it to a valid month the way it snapped 8 → 9 in the year’s hundreds slot. But that’s consistent with what Case 1 taught us, because the month slot saw all twelve values 01-12 in training - both a “1” in the tens slot and a “5” in the ones slot, so it’s likely actually just ok with this.

2) An entirely unseen format. We can also try to give the model some formats that weren’t in the data at all. Not ones that we know are different but look identical to what it’s seen - ones that are genuinely different from the set of formats we gave.

Test cases: 2014, feb 09, and 19 f 2014 and 9 f 2014

The first case is the same information it’s seen before, in a different order. We’ve given it “shorthand month, day, year” before, so this just flips the year to be first. If it’s robust in recognizing snippets of patterns it’s seen, this would do okay.

In the second 2 cases, we’re giving genuinely never before seen pieces. In 19 f 2014 we drop the “feb” for just “f”. February is the only month of the year that begins with an “f”, and 19 has only ever been a day, so maybe this will work. In the 9 f 2014 case, we go a step further, also dropping the standard “0” formatting from the day. This is quite a different case from what the model has seen, though still a human would quickly figure out what this means. The model will likely get tripped up.

test_probes = [
    ("2014, feb 09", "2014-02-09"),  # swapped ordering
    ("19 f 2014", "2014-02-19"),  # "f" as only month information
    ("9 f 2014", "2014-02-09"),  # month and day both different to parse
]

for human, expected in test_probes:
    got = generate(model, human)
    flag = "ok" if got == expected else "XX"
    print(f"[{flag}] {human:>16}  ->  {got:<12}  (wanted {expected})")
[XX]     2014, feb 09  ->  2009-02-24    (wanted 2014-02-09)
[XX]        19 f 2014  ->  2014-07-19    (wanted 2014-02-19)
[XX]         9 f 2014  ->  2044-07-20    (wanted 2014-02-09)

So, interesting.

  • 2014, feb 09 → 2009-02-24 is the interesting case. If the model picked up general patterns, we expect this one to be easy: every token snippet in it (feb, 09, 2014) is something the model has seen hundreds of times, just never with the year first. Instead, it produced something with a lot of our original information garbled. 09 from the end of the sequence, got stuck on the year. Our years normally end our inputs, so it likely sees digits at the end and thinks those are the year. The “2” and “4” from the year (first and last digits) make it to the day, again, maybe because digits at the start are expected to determine the day. The ‘feb’ copies ok, but that’s in the place the model expects it to be. So this is the most reliable piece of evidence that the model has not learned portable facts like “feb is a month” or “a four-digit number is a year” that it can recognize wherever they appear - it’s more likely learned what positions of the input correspond to positions of the output.
  • 19 f 2014 → 2014-07-19 gets close. It nails the year and the day, but gives 07 - july - for the month. It’s never seen f before, so is probably just guessing.
  • 9 f 2014 → 2044-07-20. This is surprising. You maybe wouldn’t expect this to be too different from the previous case, but now even the year has an issue, despite being within range and in its correct spot. The day and month don’t seem based on much. We’ve likely pushed it so far out of it’s comfort range here, it just fills in something sensible, not strongly based on the input.

So did the model learn any generalizable meaning? Seems like the answer is mostly no. It learned the exact conventions and formats it was shown (day-before-month, these six layouts, these spellings of the months) as surface patterns, not as facts about what a day or a month or a year actually is. There do seem to be some pretty strong positional assumptions that drive a lot of how the inputs are processed. And of course, there are times where the patterns it has learned are reusable enough that we get some surprising results, but that’s not the same thing as learning “meaning”.

📌 Note: (In general, what we’ve seen here are some small, clean instances of what’s called shortcut learning (Geirhos et al., 2020). Models latch onto whatever rule happens to solve training, with no notion that you meant something more general.)

So, what went wrong?

Well, nothing. We saw 100% accuracy on our hold-out set - the model is exceptionally well trained to the problem. You might call this “overfitting”, but it’s not, because that 100% accuracy is on hold-out data - so the model generalizes to data it’s never seen, but is like what it’s seen, incredibly well.

So then, what do we call it, when a model doesn’t perform as well as we want on cases that are different in kind from what we trained it on? We don’t call it anything - you shouldn’t expect that! We call it poorly chosen training data. Because if you knew you needed your model to perform on certain cases, you should’ve trained on them.

In a lot of ways, generalizability is more of a “nice to have” than something you can expect. You don’t get it for free, but you’re not entirely powerless, and it does seem to show up more readily in some setups than others.

One thing you can do to encourage generalizability is the same way you prevent overfitting: regularization. These techniques stop a model from committing too hard to the specifics of its training data, which also keeps its learned rules a little softer and more flexible.

And our own result hints at a different one, with a concrete experiment you could run. Recall that our model was essentially done learning by around epoch 3 - the last several epochs mostly just drove the training loss lower. A model trained for fewer epochs would carry softer priors, so the “the hundreds digit is a 0 or a 9” rule would likely be less rigidly burned in. You could try it yourself: retrain with far fewer epochs, rerun these probes, and see whether the less-fit model is the more general one. The tradeoff, though, is fit for generality. A model stopped earlier in training might have more general understanding still, but it’s also likely not fit as well. That’s why optimizing for the cases you really want is the better solution - you don’t risk underfitting in the name of getting a model that’s well generalized when that can mean it only learned weakly how to solve problem.

But even then, temper expectations. Softer priors can only help the Case 1 probes where the model had all the necessary information and was just applying a rule too hard. Stopping training early likely won’t move the needle on the Case 2 tests, because there the information is coming in in a way it’s never seen before - essentially incomplete. For those, the real lever would be what we already discussed - if you need a behavior, put it in the data.

9.4.4 Takeaways

We could keep probing specific cases for a long time, but we already made the key point: there is no simple, finite checklist that tells you how a model handles everything outside its training. The space of “things you didn’t train on” is infinite - you can’t know how it does on literally everything out of distribution.

What you should do - and what we tried to do here - is reason first. Take a hard look at your data, and ask if it really covered everything that you need the model to be able to handle. Try to understand the pattern the model could possibly have learned from the data. Assume it picked the one that was a shortcut - does that apply to the cases you need it to?

But of course “learning the pattern your model learned” is often a really hard thing to put your finger on. In this example, we had 6 distinct date formats, and we still had to do some digging to try to understand what patterns the model was really applying.

For models at larger scale, the “patterns” are very much not clear. But also, larger models have been shown to, in general, generalize better. So let’s also take a quick step back to talk about how what we’ve seen here applies to the enormous, general purpose LLMs that most of the modern field revolves around.

9.4.5 Generalizability for Large Models

As it turns out, large language models are often strikingly robust to inputs they were never explicitly trained on. Part of why is simply coverage. If you train on a large enough slice of everything people write, then a great deal of what you might think was out of distribution was actually probably somewhere in the data all along.

Sometimes though, it is different in kind. For instance, large models exhibit in-context learning (Brown et al., 2020), where they can pick up a brand new pattern from a handful of examples given in the prompt itself. Our model obviously cannot do this. But a large model, if shown two or three mm/dd examples and what to do with them in its context, can simply adapt on the spot. It’s a real, qualitative gap between the kind of ultra-small, single-purpose model we built here and what runs at the frontier.

That being said, scale does not simply dissolve the problem of out of distribution behavior and generalizability gaps. Frontier models have still been shown to latch onto shortcuts, lean on spurious correlations, and stumble on tasks requiring too much extrapolation. And whether their most impressive generalization actually reflects something like real understanding, or just incredibly broad interpolation, is honestly still an open and actively argued question.

So the core idea still stands - a model can only extend what was present in its training data. It’s just that “extending what was present” can be staggering for large models. The “patterns” inside large-scale training data are much, much more than “the ordering of the words”, and capable models can recombine the structures they learn into things that appear nowhere in their data. The ability to generalize, then, isn’t hard-capped by novelty, but it is on information. A model can’t, for instance, supply a specific fact that was never derivable from anything it was given. It won’t know your name if you don’t tell it. That is the part that, definitively, no amount of scale or cleverness will solve if the pieces aren’t there.

So how far can you expect a model to extend?

  • For information you know it never saw and could never derive from what it did see, it’s a flat no. The information simply isn’t there to find, so you can’t expect this.

  • For information you know was squarely within what it saw, it should be a reliable yes. Given a model well-trained, shown that pattern and information often, this is the case you trained for, and exactly where you expect performance.

  • But for everything in between, which is most things, with some pieces it has seen, but asked to come together in a way that was never in training - it’s a big maybe. The whole middle is always a question mark.

Bigger models tend to reach further into the “maybe” space, and smaller ones less far. So capacity genuinely matters here, but you can never quite know by how much until you look. The wide uncertain middle is answered by probing, the way we just did, not by working it out in advance.

9.5 Benchmarking

Of course, even though evaluating a modern model is not as clean as evaluating something like our toy model, it’s useful to establish some generalized evaluations to compare performance. Yes, different models will be good at different things. Yes, how far you can push them out of distribution, and in what ways, is very hard to quantify. And yes, evaluations are best done on the specific things you care about. But if I’m choosing a model to use, how do I know to pick Qwen or Mistral at 8B parameters? If I train a model, how do I know how it compares to others?

So, the standard tool for answering “how do models compare” is the benchmark: a fixed, public test set (MMLU for broad knowledge, GSM8K for grade-school math, HumanEval for coding, and hundreds more) that produces one comparable number per model. Benchmarks are useful and necessary. You need some common yardstick to track progress and compare model performance, and standardized datasets are about the best you can do for that. However, on top of the general difficulty of evaluation we’ve already seen, benchmarks have their own specific issues that make a single number a far weaker signal than it looks.

Some issues with benchmarking:

  • Contamination. Benchmarks are public, so many of their questions, or light paraphrases of those questions, routinely leak into training data. Sometimes, models score brilliantly by having effectively memorized the test rather than being able to do the task. This is pervasive and very hard to detect.
  • Goodhart’s law. “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” Benchmarks are often easy to optimize for specifically, and scores on them can climb without the underlying ability climbing with them. Models can be very good at certain benchmarks specifically, and not good in general.
  • Narrowness. A benchmark measures one skill on one distribution. Topping a math benchmark says nothing about whether a model writes well, follows instructions, stays safe, or helps with how you want to actually use it. Compressing a whole model down to one number can throw away everything that doesn’t fit that one test. So that specific performance number can be useful when the benchmark is truly a direct analog to your use case - which it very often won’t be.

This is exactly why it can be a problem to read a common headline like “tiny new 2B model beats the giant frontier model on benchmark X!” and interpret it as “tiny new 2B model must be amazing”. This almost never translates to a general “the small model is better”. It’s usually “someone optimized a small model for benchmark X,” often on data close to the test, at the cost of being worse at nearly everything the benchmark doesn’t measure.

So is there something better? Yes, but it’s exactly what we discussed, evaluating on data the model could not have seen and measuring the thing you actually care about. There are examples of this more nuanced evaluation on a larger scale, like the use of human preference comparisons, where people judge real outputs head-to-head (Chatbot Arena is the well-known public version, and much harder to game than a static test), and increasingly, a strong model used as a judge (scalable, but with biases of its own). For a holistic view across many dimensions at once rather than a single score, HELM is the canonical effort for a well-rounded benchmark.

So benchmarks are not useless. And the field is actively working to make them better. They’re a necessary common language, and good ones to help move the field forward (like MMLU and its relatives). It’s just that it’s often better used as more of a “ground floor” than a verdict. Models should at least perform well on benchmarks, usually on many of them, if they’re generally good models. But doing better on one or two, especially of the easier ones to perform well on, doesn’t tell you all that much.

10. Inspecting the Model

Now, whether your model performs great or performs poorly, there are a lot of reasons you might want to look more closely at what it’s doing when it runs a forward pass. Not just what it outputs - literally, what goes on in there, so you can pick apart how the model is actually solving the task you’ve given it.

This is a huge field in AI research - often referred to as “interpretability”, and so there is a ton that people have done to test exactly what the model comes to internally represent about the problem.

Here, we’ll just skim the surface. We’ll mostly look at attention maps and see if we can say anything about what the model learned to do through them. And for our model specifically, that’s where there’s the most to learn, as a vocabulary containing only characters won’t have the same interesting relationships between embedded words that we saw back in the first few sections anyway.

10.1 Getting and Using Attention Weights

Our MultiHeadAttention returns the attention output, but it computes the attention weights along the way. Remember, that these are an intermediate product of attention - the softmaxed (query × key) grid that says how much each query position attended to each key position. These are useful to look at exactly because they don’t yet incorporate the values from those keys. Instead, they just give us a normalized view of how much every token looks at every other token.

10.1.1 Saving the Attention Weights

To inspect them, we’ll want to actually get the values out. Fortunately, we actually already quietly added a line to stash them back when we defined MultiHeadAttention. In the MultiHeadAttention.forward, definition, we added:

attention = torch.softmax(attention_scores, dim=-1)
self.attention_weights = attention.detach()   # <- save a copy for inspection

This just creates a version of them we can pull out during a forward pass. .detach() keeps them as a plain copy, so we don’t get the whole autograd graph with them.

This means that during any forward pass we can just save them. We’ll write a function to do just that - give us back the attention weights during a forward pass:

def get_attention(model, human, iso, kind="cross"):
    """
    Run one teacher-forced pass and pull out the RAW attention weights for one of
    the model's three attention operations.
    """
    model.eval()
    src = torch.tensor([encode_src(human)], device=device)
    trg = torch.tensor([encode_trg(iso)],  device=device)
    with torch.no_grad():
        model(src, trg[:, :-1])            # one pass fills in attention_weights everywhere

    if kind == "encoder":
        mods = [blk.attention       for blk in model.encoder.layers]
    elif kind == "decoder":
        mods = [blk.attention       for blk in model.decoder.layers]
    elif kind == "cross":
        mods = [blk.cross_attention for blk in model.decoder.layers]
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown kind {kind!r} (use 'encoder', 'decoder', or 'cross')")

    # each module's weights are (1, heads, q_len, k_len); stack over layers, drop the batch dim
    A = torch.stack([m.attention_weights[0] for m in mods])   # (layers, heads, q_len, k_len)
    return A.cpu().numpy()

What this does, step by step:

  1. Puts the model in eval mode (dropout off), so what we inspect is its deterministic, deployed behavior.
  2. Runs a single teacher-forced forward pass - we hand it the whole known target so the entire output is produced at once. We don’t care about the output itself; we run the pass purely so that every attention module stashes its attention_weights. One pass fills in all of them - encoder, decoder, and cross.
  3. Then, we pick out the modules for where we actually want to get the attention from ("encoder", "decoder" self-attention, or "cross"), grabs each layer’s saved weights, and stacks them.
  4. It returns the whole thing as one array of shape (num_layers, num_heads, query_len, key_len) - which contains per layer, per head, the attention weight matrix.

When we run this function, we get back, for our chosen attention location, the query_len × key_len matrix, for every attention head, and every layer. Within this matrix, entry (i, j) is how much query position i attended to key position j. Because of the softmax, each row sums to 1 - it’s a probability distribution for how much that query - the thing that’s looking - needs to look at every key - the thing that has information to give - to find the answer. What “query” and “key” are referring to depends on the “kind” - for cross-attention, queries are output positions and keys are input positions; for the self-attentions, it’s one sequence attending to itself. When we stack all of the layers and heads together, we have the model’s entire attention story, for this one example, in a single object.

We pull all of it out of this function, but will ultimately end up slicing this into different portions depending on what we want to look at. Throughout this section, we’ll investigate what all of the different types of attention can tell us - we’ll look at the cross-attention, self in the encoder, self in the decoder, and at how they all differ with layer and head. Of course, for every part of this overall attention output that we take, we’ll explain exactly why we’re looking at that piece, and what we can tell from it.

10.1.2 Making Attention Maps

When we look at attention, we’ll look at maps. All this means is that we’ll plot the matrix itself as a heatmap, so that we can easily see the larger weights as brighter spots.

But this also means that we need to decide on a single query_len × key_len matrix to look at. In practice, this doesn’t need to mean choosing one layer and one head - we can average over heads in a layer, or even over layers, if we want to still get a single matrix out, but have it represent more than a single matrix within the model’s internals.

We will leave that choice agnostic, as throughout this section we’ll try many versions of ultimately making the maps. For now, let’s just write our simple functions that will help us visualize the matrices as maps once we have them:

def attention_labels(human, iso, kind):
    """Row (query) and column (key) tick labels for each attention kind."""
    if kind == "cross":
        # decoder output attends to encoder input: rows are what we produced, cols are what we read
        return list(iso) + ['<eos>'], list(human)
    if kind == "decoder":
        # decoder attends to itself: both axes are the decoder's own tokens
        toks = ['<bos>'] + list(iso)
        return toks, toks
    if kind == "encoder":
        # encoder attends to itself: both axes are the input characters
        return list(human), list(human)

def plot_attention(M, row_labels, col_labels, ax=None, title="",
                   ylabel="query (attending from)", xlabel="key (attended to)"):
    if ax is None:
        # size the figure to the matrix so the cells stay legible
        _, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(max(4, len(col_labels) * 0.45),
                                      max(3, len(row_labels) * 0.40)))
    # vmin/vmax pin the color scale to [0, 1] so brightness is comparable ACROSS maps
    im = ax.imshow(M, aspect='auto', cmap='viridis', vmin=0, vmax=1)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(col_labels))); ax.set_xticklabels(col_labels)   # label each column (key)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(row_labels))); ax.set_yticklabels(row_labels)   # label each row (query)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel); ax.set_ylabel(ylabel); ax.set_title(title)
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, pad=0.04)                       # weight → color key
    return ax

These two small helpers turn any 2-D slice we choose into a readable picture:

  • attention_labels defines the tick labels, to help us read directly which actual tokens are attending to each other. It depends on the “kind” of attention because the different attentions operate on different sequences (input vs output).
  • plot_attention does the visualization part. This just uses the simple matplotlib imshow, which renders the matrix as a heatmap. The one important thing for this visualization is the vmin=0, vmax=1. We pin the color scale to the full [0, 1] range, to make sure that a bright cell means the same thing in every map we make. This will be very helpful in later sections when we’re trying to directly compare maps.

So, now we’re all set up, and we’ll re-use the code we wrote here throughout the rest of Section 10.

10.2 Averaged Cross-Attention Maps

For our first stop, we’re going to look at cross attention, since it’s in a lot of ways the most intuitive type to interpret. Cross attention shows us how the decoder’s output (as query) is attending to the encoder’s input (as the keys). So, this is a direct alignment between the two sequences we care about, the human date and the ISO date it becomes.

We’re also going to do some averaging here - we’ll take just the last layer, and average over all of the heads. This is the best place to start, because the last layer is our best probe for what the model is about to output as its final answer, and averaging over the heads tells us, in general, what that layer is caring about.

10.2.1 A Success Case

Let’s start by just looking at a map and seeing what we can tell. One of the best places to start is a case where the model was successful - where the output it produces is what we want, because then we know that the attention there should be a good signal - it does what we want.

Let’s choose a date the model performed well on - pass it through to get the attention out, then take the last layer and average all of the heads:

human = "15 june 2017"
iso   = generate(model, human)
A     = get_attention(model, human, iso, "cross")   # (layers, heads, out_len, in_len)

M = A[-1].mean(0)                                   # <- the choice: last layer, averaged over heads
rows, cols = attention_labels(human, iso, "cross")
plot_attention(M, rows, cols,
               title=f"{human!r} → {iso!r}  (cross · last layer · head-avg)",
               ylabel="output (produced)", xlabel="input (read)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

So, what does a clean map tell us?

  • First, the day is a clean copy. The brightest cells in the map are between the input and output’s day numbers, so at least in a format it expects, it seems to just read the day numbers it needs from the input pretty reliably.
  • The month is better informed with more letters. The attention to the “0” and “6” from the output is generally more spread, but out over the letters of june. Interestingly, the “j” seems to motivate the “0” more strongly than it does the “6”, with the rest of “une” motivating “6” but not “0”. This would make sense - all “j” months start with a 0 in our ISO dates. But overall, all of the letters of “june” get some attention from the “0” and “6” for the month.
  • The year’s end numbers matter more than their starts. We already saw that this is likely how the model behaves from Section 9 - even though the output starts with the year, the “2” in the year output isn’t strongly motivated by the “2” in the input. And the “2” in the output, if anything, attends more to the input’s 0 (though very weakly) than it’s own 2. This already aligns with the failure modes we saw - where the year would start with a “19” or “20”, always.

It’s additionally telling when the attention is diffuse. Yes, the brighter spot for producing “0” in the output is the “0” from the year in the input - but it’s not overwhelmingly strong. In general, anytime the attention for something is diffuse, small differences can just be down to noise. Diffuse attention means the model doesn’t particularly have a strong signal to read off - but remember, thanks to the softmax, it must always put total 1 probability across the row, so you’ll always see attention somewhere.

Sometimes, that diffuse attention makes sense and is what you would expect. In this case, we’d say the attention is distributed, not really diffuse. It’s looking at different things, but has a clear picture of what it needs to look at. This is the case for the month - in this input format, there isn’t a clear single token to read from, so the attention is spread over the letters of the input month. But the “0” in the hundreds place of the year for the output is diffuse rather than attending strongly to the obvious “0” analog from the input - that tells you already that it’s not really considering that number from the input year when deciding what to go with.

10.2.2 What Values Matter

So, now let’s look at a failure case, where the model fails to get the values right, even though the information is readily available and in the exact format the model was trained to expect it in. Back in Section 9, we found that the model mangles unfamiliar years in a consistent way. When it sees 1850, it returns 1950, “correcting” an unseen hundreds digit to one it knows. So, how is that different from when it’s just given 1950?

These maps will hopefully tell us a bit more about what goes on when that happens:

humans = ["01 may 1850", "01 may 1950"]               # <- our two year cases
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(humans), figsize=(11, 4.5))

for human, ax in zip(humans, axes):
    iso = generate(model, human)                    # the model's OWN output
    A   = get_attention(model, human, iso, "cross") # (layers, heads, out_len, in_len)

    M = A[-1].mean(0)                               # same choice: last layer, head-avg
    rows, cols = attention_labels(human, iso, "cross")
    plot_attention(M, rows, cols, ax=ax,
                   title=f"{human!r} → {iso!r}",
                   ylabel="output (produced)", xlabel="input (read)")

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

So, these aren’t at all different, really! This confirms actually the hypothesis we had back in Section 9.4. Both the 19 and 18 in the output aren’t strongly motivated by their input analogs or read off from anywhere. The 9 in the output attends a teeny bit more to 9 when it’s in the input, but it’s very weak. Those first 2 digits are strong priors that the model has, and it’ll output them regardless of what the input is. Here, we see that ignoring of those digits from the input happening.

While we don’t know exactly where the “9” that overrides the “8” comes from, what we do know is that a digit the model reads straight from the input lands on its twin as a single bright cell, while a digit it overrides has nowhere to point, and smears across the row. In 1850 → 1950, the 5 and 0 lock onto the input’s 5 and 0 basically exactly as much as they do for 1950. The 9 that the model substitutes is diffuse. There’s no 9 in the input to read, because the model isn’t reading that digit at all. It’s imposing it, straight from its existing expectations. And actually, it’s doing it in both cases. The “9” never comes from the input year, it’s always just an assumption the model is making.

10.2.3 What Formatting Matters

Remember back in Section 9.4, when 2088 worked and 1912 didn’t, I said that if you tried it for a few more 20xx dates, you’d see it generally works. But we only tried two formats there. Let’s see how robust these attention patterns are for the same date in different formats.

humans = ["may 01 2088", "saturday, may 01 2088"]               # <- our two year cases
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(humans), figsize=(11, 4.5))

for human, ax in zip(humans, axes):
    iso = generate(model, human)                    # the model's OWN output
    A   = get_attention(model, human, iso, "cross") # (layers, heads, out_len, in_len)

    M = A[-1].mean(0)                               # same choice: last layer, head-avg
    rows, cols = attention_labels(human, iso, "cross")
    plot_attention(M, rows, cols, ax=ax,
                   title=f"{human!r} → {iso!r}",
                   ylabel="output (produced)", xlabel="input (read)")

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

So, this particular date is robust to formatting, too. A few things to note comparing these to other attention maps, though.

We can see that the model is doing better than just position-for-position copying. It’s robust to the day and month being flipped - it still puts the attention in the correct, and relatively the same, places when we flip the ordering.

In the spelled-out day of the week case, the model (appropriately) almost entirely ignores the “saturday”. This is also good - that information actually doesn’t motivate the ISO format at all, and the model knows not to spend much attention on it. Besides that, we see a lot of similar patterns in the attention. Though, not even the day of the week being there means the attention is a little more diffuse - we lose some of those bright yellow cells.

10.2.4 What Order Matters

Another case we encountered - when we instead gave the model the year first - it had no clue what to do with that. We weren’t totally sure what caused that, and we’ve seen it be robust to other position swaps, so can we figure out here what happened?

humans = ["2014 feb 09", "09 feb 2014"]               # <- our two year cases
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(humans), figsize=(11, 4.5))

for human, ax in zip(humans, axes):
    iso = generate(model, human)                    # the model's OWN output
    A   = get_attention(model, human, iso, "cross") # (layers, heads, out_len, in_len)

    M = A[-1].mean(0)                               # same choice: last layer, head-avg
    rows, cols = attention_labels(human, iso, "cross")
    plot_attention(M, rows, cols, ax=ax,
                   title=f"{human!r} → {iso!r}",
                   ylabel="output (produced)", xlabel="input (read)")

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

There’s something really interesting going on here, which is that the shapes of the two maps are very similar. It doesn’t matter if the year was first - the model gives the same attention pattern as if it was the day that came first. But in the previous example, we saw plenty of flexibility to swapping day and month.

But, we have some rigid formatting patterns across all of our examples, that it probably learned just as it learned our rigid slot-digit relationships. In our training data, every time an input starts with a digit, those digits are the day - that allows that to be a fixed assumption the model makes. It’s also true of the year, in our training data, no matter the format, that was always last. So it’s likely not that an edit to this specific format causes a problem - the model probably just sees a digit come in the first slot and says “ok, that’s the day”. And indeed, during training, that was a rule.

10.2.5 What Tokens Matter

One case that we saw back in Section 9.4 was 19 f 2014. The model got the day and year right, but couldn’t figure out the month, even though “f” is a unique letter to “february”. Instead, it gave us 07.

Let’s look at the attention maps for both 19 f 2014 and 19 feb 2014 and see how they’re different. Do we see stronger attention to e and b than we might expect for how tightly f should link to 02?

humans = ["19 f 2014", "19 feb 2014"]               # the examples
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(humans), figsize=(11, 4.5))

for human, ax in zip(humans, axes):
    iso = generate(model, human)                    # the model's OWN output
    A   = get_attention(model, human, iso, "cross") # (layers, heads, out_len, in_len)

    M = A[-1].mean(0)                               # same choice: last layer, head-avg
    rows, cols = attention_labels(human, iso, "cross")
    plot_attention(M, rows, cols, ax=ax,
                   title=f"{human!r} → {iso!r}",
                   ylabel="output (produced)", xlabel="input (read)")

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

So, these particular attention maps aren’t that telling. The model attends pretty strongly to f for the output month in both cases. But, when it’s just f it becomes 07, and when it’s feb, it seems that it uses the f to get 0 and the e to get 2. This is reasonable, still. “February” being the only month to start with f doesn’t mean f must shoehorn it - that also means the presence of an f shoehorns 0. Then, maybe the model got used to an e in the second slot informing 02 after an “f”. It’s hard to guess at what rule the model is making - even a shortcut rule you could think of isn’t necessarily the one it’ll take.

Let’s look at one more similar example, “july” and “june”, as they have a similar issue - with some letters matching, what does the model use?

humans = ["19 july 2014", "19 june 2014"]               # the examples
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(humans), figsize=(11, 4.5))

for human, ax in zip(humans, axes):
    iso = generate(model, human)                    # the model's OWN output
    A   = get_attention(model, human, iso, "cross") # (layers, heads, out_len, in_len)

    M = A[-1].mean(0)                               # same choice: last layer, head-avg
    rows, cols = attention_labels(human, iso, "cross")
    plot_attention(M, rows, cols, ax=ax,
                   title=f"{human!r} → {iso!r}",
                   ylabel="output (produced)", xlabel="input (read)")

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

So, we see here maybe more what we would expect, with strong attention to the l and n to decide the month number. And in both, the 0 looks again more closely at that j. So maybe, if anything, we see a similar sort of rule forming here, where the model reliably gets several month letters, and has learned to mostly pick the first digit - “0” or “1” - with the first letter, and the second digit with the rest.

So, we’ve looked at a lot of maps here. And it’s clear that sometimes, the model is reading the answer from the input, and other times, it’s diffuse. Whether or not this makes sense really just depends on case. Sometimes, it’s pooling a signal spread across several tokens (the letters of a written-out month). But other times, it’s clearly stopped consulting the input altogether and fills the slot from a learned prior (like with year digits it overrides).

But you can see, hopefully, how looking at the attention can tell you something different from what just the results do. For example, these maps reflect the model’s positional assumptions as much as the input’s content, which we saw in the case where we put the year first. But there’s also the other case, where, for instance, we were able to see how the exact letters are being considered. Other times, the maps can’t tell us much. They can’t tell us why 1912 is a problem and 2088 is ok.

That isn’t a failure of our reading or of the tool of attention maps - just a real limitation. A cross-attention map shows you where the model looks, but it can’t tell you what it does with what it finds. That can be very useful, but it’s certainly not the entire story.

10.3 Attention Per Head and Layer

For all the maps we just saw, we took the attention of the last layer and averaged over heads. This is a good general metric, but averaging wipes out differences in what the heads look at - and the whole point of heads is that they should learn to specialize. Additionally, while the last layer is easiest to interpret in that it’s the final set of weights before the output, it’s of course not the only one that matters.

So let’s try to poke a little deeper - seeing how attention differs across heads and layers - to see if we can figure out any more nuanced structure.

10.3.1 Attention Across Heads

First, instead of averaging over all of the heads in a layer, let’s just look at all of them. Fortunately, our model only has 8 heads, which isn’t so bad to just inspect individually.

We’ll still take the last layer here, but look now at every cross attention head for a working example within that layer.

human = "15 june 2017"                               # one specimen, now at full resolution
iso   = generate(model, human)
A     = get_attention(model, human, iso, "cross")    # (layers, heads, out_len, in_len)

layer = -1                                           # the choice: open up ONE layer...
rows, cols = attention_labels(human, iso, "cross")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(16, 7))      # ...and show all 8 heads of it
for h, ax in enumerate(axes.flat):
    plot_attention(A[layer, h], rows, cols, ax=ax, title=f"head {h}")
fig.suptitle(f"{human!r} → {iso!r}  (cross · last layer · each head)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

The first thing that jumps out is that the averaged map dilutes a lot of the sharpness that’s actually there. Every individual head is nearly binary - with cells either near 1.0 - put all your attention here - or otherwise 0 - don’t look at this at all. So all of the soft, diffuse signal we saw in the previous section wasn’t about heads being wishy-washy - it was precisely because the different heads are telling the model to look at different things.

Which is great, because that’s exactly what multi-head attention is supposed to provide. The heads should be able to specialize to their own part of the problem. We can see that division of labor here when we look more closely:

  • All of the heads do day copying. All except 0 have bright attention between 1 and 1 and 5 and 5 - all maps have learned that rule.
  • All heads participate in choosing the month, but different letters are in focus for different heads. All heads have at least one bright spot between one of the month letters and the first or second month digit, so it’s more of an aggregate over them that’s likely deciding month.
  • Heads 0, 1, and 2 are the ones that give the most attention to the whole year, though similar to the day, the last 2 digits of the year show up in almost all maps. The first two digits are messier. Heads 5, 6, and 7 do pick out the 2 correctly, and heads 0, 1, and 2 put the output 0 on the input 0. But those same three heads put the 2 on that input 0 as well, so they’re treating the first two digits as one block rather than copying them one by one. No single head cleanly copies both. Heads 3 and 4 attend those first 2 digits back to the month and day instead.

So our reliable pure copies show up in all heads - the second digit of the day in all, and the last digit of the year and first digit of the day in all but 1. These are the exact digits that we saw get faithfully copied again and again, and they are attended to by nearly all maps. This, of course, also shows up in our averaged maps clearly - there was always a reliable bright spot on those two digits, and we see here why - because every attention head knows those are important.

But this is also something worth pausing on, because just from this use case, it might seem like having multiple heads can hurt you. The digits that we saw the model get consistently correct are bright in every single map, and the digits that the model was shakier on are still sometimes bright - just only in one or two. Does that mean the model should have learned to make all of the heads the same?

The answer is no, of course. But let’s be precise about why not. Remember how multi-head attention actually comes back together. We averaged because that’s convenient to look at, but the model does not average its heads. Each head computes its own output, and those outputs are concatenated - laid side by side, and kept separate - and then mixed by the output projection.

So a digit that’s bright in only one head isn’t “weakly attended to” from the model’s point of view - if one head carries a clean signal into the concatenation, the output projection is free to lean on it entirely. This would be true even for the digits that are bright in every single head - the output projection is free to discount it entirely.

The problem with, for instance, the first 2 digits of the year here isn’t that they aren’t bright in enough heads, it’s more likely that they’re too bright in too many heads. The output projection could learn which head to trust to pull that digit from, but with a less clear signal, that’s harder to do. The attention to that digit is neither decisive on a broad scale (like the last digit of the year was) nor decisive within specialized heads. The signal is spread out, so picking it out is harder. And more so, it’s likely that, as we saw with those digits snapping to the 20 and 19 the model knows, it’s probably not really deciding them from the attention at all. Attention says “hey, you need to look at this thing”, but just because the model looked, doesn’t mean it does anything with it.

It’s tempting to go further and start picking apart what happens downstream, in the value mixing, the output projection, and the feed-forward layers, but those are in general much harder to look at, so we’ll skip them. And we already know what happens from the behavior we saw in Section 9: hand the model any year and it still produces a 19xx or 20xx, snapping the leading digits to what it expects no matter what the input said. So we know those digits aren’t being set by the input at all, and instead by the assumptions the model makes. The messy, conflicting head-attention here is consistent with that, and finding where exactly that information gets missed is a deep dive for a different kind of notebook!

But one more thing we can do, just to sanity check some of our claims we made from the single example above, is just look at the set of maps for a different date, in a different format. Are the heads still specialized in the same way?

human = "12/11/2017"                               # a different date choice
iso   = generate(model, human)
A     = get_attention(model, human, iso, "cross")    # (layers, heads, out_len, in_len)

layer = -1                                           # the choice: open up ONE layer...
rows, cols = attention_labels(human, iso, "cross")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(16, 7))      # ...and show all 8 heads of it
for h, ax in enumerate(axes.flat):
    plot_attention(A[layer, h], rows, cols, ax=ax, title=f"head {h}")
fig.suptitle(f"{human!r} → {iso!r}  (cross · last layer · each head)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

There are some consistent things these heads are doing. First off, the day digits and the final digit in the year are strongly attended in all but 0, same as in the last example. That’s expected. But notice where the specialization is happening. Heads 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7, are where the month is most straightforwardly attended, which is similar to where “june” had some of the strongest signal on “j” and “u”. So those heads probably are the ones most responsible for the month, it’s just that when the month is spelled out, that shows up in more pieces than it does for the clean format we have here.

But… you also might look at this and say: “Sure, I see some specializing, but if a lot of what is done well just shows up as the same sort of map, do we even need eight heads?” And that in general is a very fair question - it’s actually been shown that trained models often do carry more heads than they strictly need. But - you can’t really conclude it from maps like this alone. A redundant (or, even a flat) head isn’t necessarily not doing anything. Near-redundant and near-uniform attention both still produce an output, and a head can carry its real contribution through its values and the output projection rather than through the specific pattern we can see. On top of that, as we touched on here, different inputs may activate different heads more or less. Some heads can be specialists for a specific formats or values, and just don’t have much nuanced to say about some specific case.

So asking “do we need this head” is an important question - and too much attention head redundancy or consistently flat maps could be an early sign. But it’s not a diagnosis. To really determine if the head is useless, we’d need to try to remove it and see if the model misses it - a technique called head pruning. That’s again, way out of scope for this notebook, so we’ll just say that for those heads, we can’t really tell what it is exactly they provide from maps alone.

10.3.2 Attention Across Layers

The next thing we’ll do is look at how attention differs across layers. The intuition for different heads is that they’re meant to specialize across different features. The intuition behind layers is that they tend to sharpen features - earlier layers will look more broadly, and later layers will be more focused. Let’s see if that’s true.

We’ll return to the average over the heads, to try to get that aggregate sense again for what attention is doing. So we’ll just see what the average attention looked like at each layer depth.

human = "15 june 2017"                                  # the same specimen as 10.3.1
iso   = generate(model, human)
A     = get_attention(model, human, iso, "cross")      # (layers, heads, out_len, in_len)
rows, cols = attention_labels(human, iso, "cross")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, A.shape[0], figsize=(5.5 * A.shape[0], 4.5))
for l, ax in zip(range(A.shape[0]), axes):
    plot_attention(A[l].mean(0), rows, cols, ax=ax, title=f"layer {l}")
fig.suptitle(f"{human!r} → {iso!r}  (cross · head-avg · each layer)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

So, the intuition holds for layer 0, but layer 1 is actually already pretty sharp. As we get further in depth, overall the structure tightens. Layer 0 is a pretty broad, low-contrast wash, with a bit of focus on the year. The model at this point is gathering information widely, not committing to anything yet.

But by layer 1, we see the model start to hone in on the days, a little bit across the month, and the last 2 digits of the year. By layer 2, the second digit of the day has fully sharpened, and more attention has collected around key letters of the month (the “n”) and year. As we saw splitting into heads, at least for the month that’s probably more about a real separation of signal, not it being indecisive.

It should also be more obvious now why we chose the last layer, for the most part, to investigate attention maps. In the final layer, the model is more decisive about where to put its focus, as those attention weights are more directly influencing the output. In earlier layers, attention is so spread because attention heads are looking at many different things, gathering more information, and it can be hard to determine where the key attention points will end up.

But, just while we’re here, let’s confirm that with one more set of plots. Let’s look at all of the heads in the first layer instead of the last.

human = "15/06/2017"                                 # a different date choice
iso   = generate(model, human)
A     = get_attention(model, human, iso, "cross")    # (layers, heads, out_len, in_len)

layer = 0                                            # the choice: open up ONE layer...
rows, cols = attention_labels(human, iso, "cross")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(16, 7))      # ...and show all 8 heads of it
for h, ax in enumerate(axes.flat):
    plot_attention(A[layer, h], rows, cols, ax=ax, title=f"head {h}")
fig.suptitle(f"{human!r} → {iso!r}  (cross · first layer · each head)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

You might’ve expected these to look diffuse, but even early on, the heads are learning to put their attention in specific places. It’s just that they’re grabbing for more things across heads. Look at the 5 in the day. Across heads, it attends to: the 5 in the day (itself) (heads 0 and 7), the 0 in the month (head 1 and 5), the 1 in the day (heads 2 and 3), the 6 in the month (head 4), the / after the day (head 5), and the 7 in the year (head 6) - a far cry from the decisive 5 \(→\) 5 we see in the last layer.

But is that wrong? No! Earlier layers in the model are still going to be transformed by later layers, so their focus is more on prep work. This is clear in the structure they do have. Head 5 spreads attention all over the place. Consistent verticals, like heads 2, and 6 have, seem to be mostly about attending the digit in that slot to everything, making sure all of the output knows about it. Early structure prefers this type of attention over clean copies, because before the model can copy the right digit, it has to work out which part of the input is the day, the month, the year - and that’s a matter of relating positions to each other. This goes back to something that we’ve talked about many times in this notebook - the decoder itself still has a job of understanding to do, and we can see it here. Attention like this is the model understanding how the input structure needs to relate to its output, which is a key prerequisite to making decisions that depend on that structure.

So, all layers of attention are doing something important. It’s just that earlier layers can be harder to interpret, because they’re informing later layers of the model more so than the output from the model. It’s harder for us to say exactly how this structure will return a result, but we can trust that it’s important for the model, because the model has decidedly honed in on those features.

10.4 Self-Attention Maps

When we read the cross-attention maps, some things came through crisply - the day, the month. But other parts were stubbornly diffuse, right where you’d least expect it: the leading digits of the year, which the model isn’t sourcing from the input even though an obvious source is sitting right there. That left a loose end. The model isn’t guessing randomly - hand it the same date and it produces the same output every time, so something is deciding those digits. If it isn’t the input, where is it?

The only other thing the decoder has to look at is its own output so far - the characters it has already produced. That’s exactly what the decoder’s self-attention sees. So this is the natural place to chase the loose end down: if the hundreds digit isn’t read from the input, maybe it’s read from the thousands digit the model just wrote. Let’s look.

(There are two self-attentions - one in the encoder, one in the decoder - so we’ll look at both. The encoder’s is the quieter of the two; the decoder’s is where our loose end might get tied up.)

10.4.1 Encoder Self-Attention Maps

Let’s start by looking at the encoder’s self-attention, because it comes first in the model’s flow. Before the decoder generates anything, the encoder passes the input through its own attention, trying to build a rich representation of the input. Its job is to let each character of the date gather context from the rest.

This means, unlike cross-attention where we expect to see where the output is coming from, we expect to just be able to tell what tokens are contextualized by other ones. The encoder should be where the input gets organized. So, for instance, where in cross attention we saw that the output could read the month off just a couple of the letters of june - we’d expect that the encoder does some work to gather the letters of “june” into some coherent signal - maybe we’ll see attention across those letters to each other. That being said, expect these maps to be quieter than cross-attention, because the job the encoder has to do is less “clean”, and encoding naturally means spreading across more of the input.

We’re going to go back to looking at averages first, as interpreting a single map is always cleanest. And, we’ll go back to the last layer, where there’s theoretically the clearest signal to see.

# encoder self - the full square (no mask), + the month-pooling check
human = "15 june 2017"
iso   = generate(model, human)
A     = get_attention(model, human, iso, "encoder")   # (layers, heads, in_len, in_len)

M = A[-1].mean(0)
rows, cols = attention_labels(human, iso, "encoder")
plot_attention(M, rows, cols,
               title=f"{human!r}  (encoder self · last layer · head-avg)",
               ylabel="input (attending from)", xlabel="input (attended to)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

So, the encoder’s self-attention is a pretty quiet map, just as we thought it might be. But this map is very flat - we really can’t pick out anything distinct at all besides a little on the day, a little on the year, and some spread for “june”.

But, we saw in the last section how an unstructured map like this might just mean head-averaging killed our signal and not that it’s not there, so let’s take a look at the heads:

human = "15 june 2017"
iso   = generate(model, human)
A     = get_attention(model, human, iso, "encoder")    # (layers, heads, out_len, in_len)

layer = -1                                             # last layer again
rows, cols = attention_labels(human, iso, "encoder")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(16, 7))        # now show all 8 heads of it
for h, ax in enumerate(axes.flat):
    plot_attention(A[layer, h], rows, cols, ax=ax, title=f"head {h}")
fig.suptitle(f"{human!r} → {iso!r}  (encoder self · last layer · each head)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

So we do see some structure here. Still not as strong and crisp as the cross-attention, but these maps are clearly serving a purpose.

  • There are a lot of vertical stripes here, which work to pool together nearby information. Heads 6 and 7 aggregate more so over the month, where heads 3, 5, and 7 seem to pull together year information.
  • Some do lock digits onto themselves or to their neighbors, but different ones handle different digits. So the same division of labor we saw in the cross-attention grid shows up on the input side too.

So, the encoder is organizing its input, it’s just not as obvious. It does some work to pool together some information, and anchor some digits or segments. The average blurs what the specialists are doing, but they’re there.

10.4.2 Decoder Self-Attention

Now, the decoder. The decoder’s attention is output-to-output, so here we’ll see how each new token the model generates attends to the tokens it has already generated. Besides the input, which we looked at in cross-attention, this is where the model gets the other part of its decision-making from.

This is where that loose end about the years might finally get tied. We saw that the year’s leading digits don’t come from the input, because cross-attention went diffuse where an obvious source was sitting. So if they come from anywhere the model can see, it’s from the output it has already produced. We’ll hopefully see in these maps, if we can figure out where the year “correction” might stem from.

A few things to note before we look at this. First, these maps will be triangular, because the causal masking doesn’t allow looking ahead. Second is about how we have to read these, because it’s different from the ones we’ve read so far. For the decoder, each row’s attention is the computation that produces the next token. So to ask where a digit in the output (attended to) comes from, you look at the previous digit’s row. Essentially, say I want to understand what motivated the final digit in the year 2017. I’d look at what the 7 “attended to” on the x-axis, and follow it up to the row that corresponds to 1 from the “attending from”, because each new token is generated from the attentions of the previous.

Finally, we should expect this to carry more visible structure than the encoder. Since in the decoder, the final layer is back to being right before the output, this is closer to an actual decision.

# decoder self - the triangle; a match case beside an override case
humans = ["15 june 2017", "01 may 1850"]               # <- your match + override strings
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(humans), figsize=(11, 5))

for human, ax in zip(humans, axes):
    iso = generate(model, human)
    A   = get_attention(model, human, iso, "decoder")  # (layers, heads, out_len, out_len)
    M   = A[-1].mean(0)
    rows, cols = attention_labels(human, iso, "decoder")
    plot_attention(M, rows, cols, ax=ax,
                   title=f"{human!r} → {iso!r}",
                   ylabel="output (attending from)", xlabel="output (attended to)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

The decoder’s attention is dominated by, if anything, just a generic autoregressive pattern. Tokens mostly lean on a few tokens right before it. That’s a sensible thing for a generator to do (keep track of where you are), but it isn’t specific to any of the tokens themselves. Some rows are just generally, uninterestingly, spread, which doesn’t tell us very much.

Here, we also put a map where we successfully copied the year, and see that the map has nearly the same shape as when we didn’t successfully copy the year. Of course though, by now we know not to trust the averaged maps as an absolute verdict, so let’s go the step further and look at the heads themselves:

human = "15 june 2017"
iso   = generate(model, human)
A     = get_attention(model, human, iso, "decoder")    # (layers, heads, out_len, in_len)

layer = -1                                             # last layer again
rows, cols = attention_labels(human, iso, "decoder")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(16, 7))        # now show all 8 heads of it
for h, ax in enumerate(axes.flat):
    plot_attention(A[layer, h], rows, cols, ax=ax, title=f"head {h}")
fig.suptitle(f"{human!r} → {iso!r}  (decoder · last layer · each head)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
# decoder self - the triangle; a match case beside an override case
human = "15 june 1850"
iso   = generate(model, human)
A     = get_attention(model, human, iso, "decoder")    # (layers, heads, out_len, in_len)

layer = -1                                             # last layer again
rows, cols = attention_labels(human, iso, "decoder")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(16, 7))        # now show all 8 heads of it
for h, ax in enumerate(axes.flat):
    plot_attention(A[layer, h], rows, cols, ax=ax, title=f"head {h}")
fig.suptitle(f"{human!r} → {iso!r}  (decoder · last layer · each head)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

So, it’s a lot to look at, but once again, a specific hypothesis is best confirmed by looking at all of the heads, because the average can wash them out, and we see some real structure from this view. I’ll just point out a few things.

The biggest difference is how head 3 acts on these two cases. In the case of the year it gets right - 15 june 2017 - this head is diagonal over the year digits - that pure autoregressive “look at the previous digit for the next”. But for the 15 june 1850 case, we see a vertical line over the <bos> or the 1 instead. Heads 2, 4, and 6 seem to do a better job attending to the previous token, the autoregressive behavior, than the 1850 case, which you might expect is doing more guessing. Most other heads are largely the same - and we do have the same format and day/month combination here.

So, what can we tell from what we see? Well, we can see that attention is different when the model is inventing rather than copying, but we still don’t get to see where the invented digit is coming from. Head 3 “messing up” and attending to <bos> isn’t a “source” of information so much as it’s a fallback. And heads 2, 4, and 6 all more cleanly attending to the token behind them might just mean the model has more license to “make it up”, based on what it does with this information downstream. We really can’t say for sure what actually happens to this information. All we can really tell is that between cross-attention, which never locked onto the input year, and self-attention, which pretty well follows the autoregressive pattern in both cases, though for different heads, - the model doesn’t clearly just “get” the information from somewhere. The 9 comes from somewhere else that attention maps can’t tell us.

10.5 Attention Maps Come to Life

Every map we’ve looked at so far has been a snapshot from the finished model. This is useful to figure out what the model ended up with, but of course, a model’s attention learns and adapts during training. Elements that are obvious in the final map, like the clean digit copies, the specialized heads, the diffuse year, are all features that form during training.

So one more thing we can do, is actually watch it form. If we look at how attention takes shape over time, we can see it form, in real time, what eventually become the rigid rules we saw in the final maps.

10.5.1 Attention Forming Over Training

When we were training, I saved off frequent checkpoints and said we’d use them later. This is what we were saving them for. Looking at how attention forms over time means we need to be able to look at what attention looked like during previous forward passes, which are lost if we don’t save the checkpoints. Here, we can just re-run our calculation through those checkpoints to see how attention evolved.

We’ll just look here at cross-attention, as that’s the most telling, and again the average over heads and last layer so we just have one object to look at.

📌 Note: Even if you reloaded my model checkpoint earlier, that does not have all of the checkpoints needed to create this visualization. So don’t re-run this cell unless you’ve also re-run this whole notebook so far, with a newly trained model and your own checkpoints folder.

human = "15 june 2017"
iso   = "2017-06-15"                     # FIXED target, teacher-forced at EVERY frame
rows, cols = attention_labels(human, iso, "cross")   # computed once; identical every frame

CKPT_DIR = "checkpoints"
manifest = json.load(open(f"{CKPT_DIR}/manifest.json"))
frame_paths = []
for step, path in manifest:
    model.load_state_dict(torch.load(path, map_location=device)); model.eval()
    M = get_attention(model, human, iso, "cross")[-1].mean(0)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
    plot_attention(M, rows, cols, ax=ax, title=f"step {step:>5d}    {human!r} → {iso!r}")
    fp = f"{CKPT_DIR}/frame_{step:06d}.png"
    fig.savefig(fp, dpi=110)             # fixed figsize+dpi, NO bbox_inches='tight'
    plt.close(fig)
    frame_paths.append(fp)

frames = [imageio.imread(fp) for fp in frame_paths]
imageio.mimsave("attention_forming.mp4", frames + [frames[-1]] * 8, fps=2)
WARNING:imageio_ffmpeg:IMAGEIO FFMPEG_WRITER WARNING: input image is not divisible by macro_block_size=16, resizing from (660, 550) to (672, 560) to ensure video compatibility with most codecs and players. To prevent resizing, make your input image divisible by the macro_block_size or set the macro_block_size to 1 (risking incompatibility).
data = base64.b64encode(open("attention_forming.mp4", "rb").read()).decode()
HTML(f'<video src="data:video/mp4;base64,{data}" controls loop autoplay muted width="600"></video>')

So you’ll notice that it actually hones in really fast. We have many more checkpoints saved earlier in the model here, so while we do see the first several steps represent still the largely untrained model, the attention signal forms very quickly. It zeroes in on day-to-day, month-to-month, and year-to-year in just a few hundred steps. The day is the quickest signal to be firmly decided, with the month and year continuing to change their shapes slightly until more towards the end. Though of course, a good amount of that is due to natural randomness, and some of the effect is washed out from the averaging.

But one question this does raise, is why does this seem to settle so fast? And it’s really because, in this case, the problem really is that easy. “Copy the digit” is about the simplest thing you can ask a transformer to do, so it makes a lot of sense that the model has essentially decided what it needs to look at by the end of the first epoch. A lot of what we see after that really is just some randomness, not the model changing its mind on what to look at.

10.5.2 Entropy Curves

The video makes the sharpening obvious to the eye, but “obvious to the eye” isn’t something you can quantify. Fortunately, this effect is something we can quantify fairly easily.

Remember what a single row of an attention map really is: a probability distribution. Every query spreads a total of 1.0 across the keys it could look at. A sharp row dumps almost all of that 1.0 onto one or two keys, so the model is sure where to look. A diffuse row spreads it thinly across many, with no strong preference. So “how sharp is this attention” is really “how concentrated is this distribution,” and that’s a question with a standard answer.

That answer is entropy. For a distribution with probabilities \(p_1, p_2, \dots\) over the keys, \[ H = -\sum_i p_i \log p_i \]

If all the weight lands on a single key (\(p=1\) there, \(0\) elsewhere), the sum is \(0\), so zero entropy means perfectly concentrated. If the weight is spread perfectly evenly across \(n\) keys (\(p = 1/n\) each), the entropy hits its maximum, \(\log n\). This gives one number per row, so to get a single number for a whole map, we average the entropy over all the query rows.

We’ll also plot two things here. First, the entropy of the head-averaged map, which is useful, but we know the blend is not the sharpest signal. So we’ll also plot the entropy of the single sharpest head (the most concentrated specialist at that moment). The average says how focused the overall picture looks, and the second says how focused the model’s most specialized individual head has gotten.

human, iso = "15 june 2017", "2017-06-15"
manifest = json.load(open(f"{CKPT_DIR}/manifest.json"))

def row_entropy(M):                       # M: (q,k), each row sums to 1
    p = np.clip(M, 1e-9, 1)
    return (-(p * np.log(p)).sum(1)).mean()   # mean entropy over query rows (nats)

steps, avg_H, best_H = [], [], []
for step, path in manifest:
    model.load_state_dict(torch.load(path, map_location=device)); model.eval()
    A = get_attention(model, human, iso, "cross")
    steps.append(step)
    avg_H.append(row_entropy(A[-1].mean(0)))
    best_H.append(min(row_entropy(A[-1, h]) for h in range(A.shape[1])))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
ax.plot(steps, avg_H,  'o-', label="head-average")
ax.plot(steps, best_H, 'o-', label="sharpest head")
ax.axhline(np.log(len(human)), ls='--', c='gray', lw=1, label="uniform (diffuse)")
ax.set_xscale('symlog')                       # so step 0 shows on a log-ish axis
ax.set_xlim([0,10000])
ax.set_xlabel("training step"); ax.set_ylabel("attention entropy (nats)")
ax.set_title("Cross-attention sharpening")
ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

So a few things. First, the drop is a cliff, just like we saw. After around 200-300 steps, it starts to plummet. By 1000 steps, not much more additional sharpening happens overall, though the sharpest head does continue to get sharper. With 50,000 examples at batch size 16, one epoch is 50000 / 16 = 3,125 steps - so even by 1/3 into the first epoch, the model has decided most of what information it needs to get, from where.

The second thing is that gap between these two lines is exactly what we already saw with head averaging - the sharpest single head plunges far lower than the head-average, because the average blends different specialists, but the heads are specializing strongly.

The overall speed here acts as a kind of a difficulty gauge. Our toy locks in almost instantly because its task is trivial.
